title: Exploring space: why a satellite never lands, and what it costs to put one up

summary.text: A rocket only has to climb about 400 kilometres to reach the space station, a little further than the road from Chennai to Bengaluru. Yet the rocket is as tall as a ten-storey building and about nine tenths of its weight is fuel. The puzzle is that going up is the easy part. Staying up is hard, because the station is falling all the time and keeps missing the ground, by moving sideways at about 8 kilometres every second. Your child rolls marbles off a table to see how falling and missing fit together, then loads a balloon rocket to see why every kilogram costs so much fuel. Along the way come telescopes that see in radio waves and infrared, the long curved road Chandrayaan-3 took to the Moon, and what space does to a body.
summary.art: A marble rolling off a table edge in three curved paths of different lengths, and above the table a faint picture of the Earth with a satellite circling it and a cannon on a mountain.

intro.hook: Throw a ball as hard as you can. It curves down and lands. Throw it harder and it lands farther away. Now imagine a throw so fast that the ground curves away as quickly as the ball falls. Where does the ball land?
intro.text: It never lands. That ball would circle the Earth, falling all the time and always missing. This is exactly what the space station does. In this unit you roll marbles off a table and watch speed decide where they land. You load a balloon rocket with paper clips and find out why rockets must carry fuel to lift their own fuel. You build a telescope from two lenses. You draw the orbits of satellites to scale on the floor. And you follow the 40-day journey of India's Chandrayaan-3, which went round the Earth again and again before it ever reached the Moon.
intro.art: A child at a table edge letting a marble roll down a folded card ramp, with a sheet of newspaper on the floor below showing three wet marble marks at different distances.

outcomes: I can explain that a satellite is always falling, and stays up because it moves sideways fast enough to keep missing the ground.
I can say about how fast a satellite must move to stay in orbit, and why a rocket spends most of its effort on sideways speed and not on height.
I can use my balloon rocket results to explain why a lighter rocket gains more speed, and why rockets drop their empty stages.
I can explain why a higher orbit is slower than a lower one, and why one special high orbit makes a satellite hang over the same spot.
I can explain that a wider telescope both collects more light and shows finer detail, and say how radio and space telescopes see what our eyes cannot.
I can say what weightlessness, radiation and space junk do to people and machines, and how each danger is handled.
I can describe an Indian mission such as Mangalyaan or Chandrayaan-3 from launch to arrival, and say why the journey took many days.

terms.meaning: The curved path of a thing that is falling around a planet or a star and keeps missing it.
terms.example: The International Space Station orbits the Earth about every 90 minutes.
terms.art: A dotted circle round the Earth with a space station on it and a small arrow showing it moving sideways.

terms.meaning: Falling with nothing holding you up. A thing in free fall feels no weight, even though gravity is pulling it.
terms.example: At the top of a jump, for a moment you feel light. Astronauts on the space station are in free fall all the time.
terms.art: A girl at the top of a jump on a trampoline with her arms out, and the ground far below.

terms.meaning: How high something is above the ground or the sea.
terms.example: The space station flies at an altitude of about 400 kilometres.
terms.art: A tall straight ruler beside the Earth with marks for a plane, the space station and a satellite.

terms.meaning: The sideways speed a thing needs to keep missing the ground and stay in orbit. Close to the Earth it is about 8 kilometres every second.
terms.example: A Vande Bharat train runs at about 160 kilometres an hour. A satellite near the Earth is about 170 times faster.
terms.art: A train on a track and above it a satellite with a long arrow, the satellite arrow much longer.

terms.meaning: The push that an engine gives to a rocket. It comes from the gas thrown out of the back.
terms.example: A balloon that is let go flies off because its escaping air gives it thrust.
terms.art: A balloon flying one way with air streaming out of its neck the other way.

terms.meaning: Everything a rocket burns and throws out of its engine, which means the fuel and the oxygen together.
terms.example: Most of a rocket's weight at lift-off is propellant.
terms.art: A cut-away rocket with two big tanks that fill most of its body, one for fuel and one for oxygen.

terms.meaning: The useful thing a rocket carries into space, such as a satellite, a lander or a crew.
terms.example: The payload of Chandrayaan-3's rocket was the spacecraft that carried Vikram and Pragyan.
terms.art: The nose cone of a rocket opened like a shell, with a satellite inside.

terms.meaning: One section of a rocket, with its own tanks and engine. It is dropped when its tanks are empty.
terms.example: India's PSLV has four stages.
terms.art: A rocket in three colours with arrows showing each section falling away in turn.

terms.meaning: How fast the gas leaves the engine. For the rockets we use now it is about 3 to 4 kilometres a second.
terms.example: A rocket that throws gas out faster gets more speed from the same amount of propellant.
terms.art: A rocket engine with a long jet and a speed arrow of 3 to 4 kilometres a second beside it.

terms.meaning: The speed a thing needs to leave a planet for good, with no more push. For the Earth it is about 11 kilometres every second.
terms.example: Mangalyaan had to leave the Earth's pull behind before it could travel to Mars.
terms.art: A ball thrown up from the Earth at three speeds, with the fastest path leaving the picture.

terms.meaning: A circle about 36,000 kilometres above the equator. A satellite there takes exactly one day to go round, so it stays above the same spot on the ground.
terms.example: The dish on a rooftop points at a satellite in this orbit.
terms.art: The Earth seen from above the North Pole with a satellite always over the same city and a dish pointing at it.

terms.meaning: The floating feeling of having no weight. It happens in free fall, and scientists also call it microgravity.
terms.example: On the space station, a pen let go in the air just stays there.
terms.art: An astronaut floating with a pen and a notebook drifting beside her.

terms.meaning: Energy that travels through space as waves or very fast tiny pieces. A lot of the radiation from the Sun and stars can harm living bodies.
terms.example: The Earth's air and its magnetic field protect us from most space radiation.
terms.art: Sun rays arriving at the Earth, with a bubble round the Earth stopping most of them.

terms.meaning: Broken satellites, empty rocket stages and tiny flecks of paint that still circle the Earth. Also called space junk.
terms.example: A fleck of paint moving at orbital speed can crack a window.
terms.art: The Earth with a thin cloud of tiny dots around it and a satellite with a small crack in a panel.

terms.meaning: The distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres. It measures distance, not time.
terms.example: The nearest star after the Sun is a little more than 4 light-years away.
terms.art: A ray of light crossing a long line marked in years, from the Sun to a faraway star.

terms.meaning: A telescope that catches radio waves from space with a big dish. Radio waves pass through clouds, so it works day and night.
terms.example: The Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope near Pune has 30 dishes, each 45 metres wide.
terms.art: Several huge white dishes in a field near Pune, all pointing at the same patch of sky.

terms.meaning: Light that our eyes cannot see, which warm things give out. It is the light that feels like heat.
terms.example: The James Webb Space Telescope looks at the sky in infrared.
terms.art: A hand glowing in an infrared picture next to a normal picture of the same hand.

terms.meaning: How much fine detail a picture or a telescope can show. A wider telescope opening gives finer detail.
terms.example: The two headlights of a faraway lorry look like one light, until you look through binoculars.
terms.art: Two close dots that look like one blurred dot, and the same two dots clearly apart in a sharper picture.

terms.meaning: The short time when the planets are placed so that a trip needs the least fuel.
terms.example: Mars launch windows come about every 26 months. Mangalyaan used one in late 2013.
terms.art: Earth and Mars on two circles round the Sun, with a curved path joining them at the right moment.

terms.meaning: The planned path of a rocket or spacecraft through space.
terms.example: Mangalyaan's trajectory curved round the Sun from the Earth to Mars.
terms.art: A curved dotted line from the Earth to Mars with small marks for the engine burns.

explanations.concept: Falling sideways: what an orbit is
explanations.definition: An orbit is a fall that never ends. A satellite falls towards the Earth all the time, but it moves sideways so fast that the Earth's ground curves away as quickly as the satellite falls.
explanations.description: Drop a ball and it falls straight down. Throw it sideways and it falls in a curve and lands farther away. Throw it faster and it lands even farther. The Earth is round, so the ground curves away below a flying ball. Over every 8 kilometres, the ground curves down by about 5 metres. A ball falls about 5 metres in its first second. So a ball that also moves 8 kilometres sideways in that second would find the ground just as far below as before. It keeps falling and keeps missing. That is an orbit. Eight kilometres a second is far faster than any throw, so only a rocket can reach it. Isaac Newton imagined this more than 300 years ago, with a cannon on a very high mountain.
examples: A stone thrown gently lands at your feet. A cricket ball thrown hard lands far down the field. A satellite is thrown so fast that it never lands.
The Moon is also falling around the Earth, and it takes about 27 days to go round once.
The space station and the astronaut beside her fall together, so she floats next to the wall.
explanations.art: A cannon on a high mountain firing three shots: one landing near, one landing far, and one going right round the round Earth.
explanations.context: This card explains the big idea of the unit: that staying up in orbit is really falling and missing.

explanations.concept: How fast, and how long a lap
explanations.definition: A satellite close to the Earth must move sideways at about 8 kilometres a second, which is about 28,000 kilometres an hour, to stay in orbit.
explanations.description: The fastest train in India runs at about 160 kilometres an hour. The space station is about 170 times faster. One lap of the Earth at the station's height is about 42,000 kilometres long. At that speed a lap takes about 90 minutes. So the crew sees about 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every day. Here is the surprise about rockets. To rise 400 kilometres needs only about a third of the speed that staying up there needs. So a rocket climbs through the thick air quickly, then tips over and spends most of its effort gaining sideways speed. Height is easy. Speed is the hard part.
examples: 28,000 kilometres an hour is about 460 kilometres every minute.
The station crosses the whole length of India, about 3,000 kilometres, in about 6 minutes.
A rocket from Sriharikota heads out over the sea towards the east, in the same direction as the Earth turns, to borrow some of the Earth's own spin.
explanations.art: A tall rocket path that first goes straight up and then bends over into a long flat curve above the sea.
explanations.context: This card is about how fast a satellite must go, and why a rocket mostly builds sideways speed.

explanations.definition: The higher a satellite orbits, the slower it moves and the longer one lap takes, because the Earth's pull is weaker farther away.
explanations.description: The space station is 400 kilometres up and takes 90 minutes for a lap. Navigation satellites such as the American GPS ones are about 20,000 kilometres up and take about 12 hours. At about 36,000 kilometres, a lap takes 24 hours, exactly the time the Earth takes to turn once. A satellite there over the equator seems to hang still above one spot, so it is called geostationary. This is why a TV dish on a roof can stay pointed at one place in the sky. The Moon is 384,000 kilometres away and takes about 27 days. Speeds drop too. The station moves at about 7.7 kilometres a second, a geostationary satellite at about 3, and the Moon at about 1.
examples: India's INSAT and GSAT satellites sit in geostationary orbit and carry TV, phone and weather signals.
A satellite that is a little lower than another one will slowly overtake it.
To move a satellite to a higher orbit, an engine speeds it up at the right moment, and afterwards it settles into a slower, higher circle.

Katherine Johnson, an American mathematician, worked out paths for the first American crewed space flights in the early 1960s, and checked the computer's numbers by hand for John Glenn's orbit flight.
explanations.art: Three circles round the Earth for the space station, a navigation satellite and a geostationary satellite, with lap times of 90 minutes, 12 hours and 24 hours.
explanations.context: This card is about how the height of an orbit decides the speed and the time of a lap.

explanations.concept: A rocket carries fuel to lift its fuel
explanations.definition: A rocket speeds up by throwing its own gas backwards. A heavier rocket needs more push for the same speed, so most of a rocket's weight at lift-off is propellant.
explanations.description: The gas leaves a rocket engine at about 3 to 4 kilometres a second. The rocket needs about 9 kilometres a second in all to reach orbit, because gravity and air slow it on the way up. That is more than twice the speed of the gas. So the rocket must throw away most of its own weight to get there. Every extra kilogram of payload needs more fuel to lift it, and then more fuel to lift that fuel. For a big rocket, around nine tenths of the weight at lift-off is propellant. The satellite on top may be only a few percent of the weight, or less than one percent. This is why rockets drop their empty tanks. A stage that is empty is dead weight, and dropping it makes the rest much easier to speed up.
examples: PSLV weighs hundreds of tonnes at lift-off, and the satellites it carries weigh only a few tonnes.
A balloon rocket with paper clips taped on goes a shorter distance than one with none.
A rocket that dropped nothing would need to be far bigger to reach orbit.
explanations.art: A rocket drawn in slices: a very thick slice for propellant, a thin slice for the rocket body and a tiny slice at the top for the payload.
explanations.context: This card explains why rockets are so big and why they are built in stages.

explanations.concept: Climbing to the Moon in small steps
explanations.definition: A spacecraft can raise its orbit by firing its engine at the right moment to speed up. A series of small burns can lift it from a low orbit all the way to the Moon.
explanations.description: Chandrayaan-3 was launched on 14 July 2023 and landed on 23 August 2023, 40 days later. The rocket did not throw it straight at the Moon. It left the spacecraft in a long oval orbit round the Earth. Over the next days, ISRO fired the spacecraft's engine several times when it was closest to the Earth. Each burn stretched the oval farther out. On 1 August a last burn sent it off towards the Moon. On 5 August the Moon's gravity caught it, and it began to orbit the Moon. More burns lowered that orbit step by step, until the lander separated and came down. A single big push would have needed a much bigger rocket. Many small burns trade time for rocket size. Mangalyaan did the same round the Earth in 2013 before it left for Mars.
examples: From 14 July to 23 August is 40 days: 17 days left in July, and 23 more in August.
Mangalyaan was launched on 5 November 2013. It reached Mars orbit on 24 September 2014, about 320 days later.
Mars launch windows come about every 26 months, so Mangalyaan could not simply wait a week and go.
explanations.art: The Earth with an oval orbit that grows wider in steps, then a curved line to the Moon with smaller circles round the Moon.
explanations.context: This card is about how a spacecraft really travels to the Moon: in many steps and not in one throw.

explanations.definition: A telescope's opening does two jobs. It collects more light, and it shows finer detail. Both get better as the opening gets wider.
explanations.description: In the half-lens test of Class 3, a bigger lens made a brighter picture. A bigger opening also makes a sharper picture. Light spreads out a little as it goes through any opening, and a narrow opening blurs fine detail more than a wide one. A telescope with a wide mirror can split two stars that look like one to a small telescope. Magnifying is a separate thing. A telescope with two lenses magnifies by the long focal length of the big front lens divided by the short focal length of the eyepiece. A lens that bends light to a point 100 centimetres away and an eyepiece that bends it to a point 2 centimetres away gives 50 times. But magnifying a blurry picture only gives a bigger blur. Galileo used lenses in 1609. Isaac Newton built a telescope with a curved mirror in about 1668. Very big lenses sag under their own weight, and a mirror can be supported from behind. So all the biggest telescopes use mirrors.
examples: The Hubble Space Telescope has a mirror 2.4 metres wide.
The James Webb Space Telescope has a mirror 6.5 metres wide, made of 18 six-sided pieces.
No telescope on or near the Earth can show the flags left on the Moon, because they are far too small to see from so far away.
explanations.art: Two telescopes side by side, a narrow one showing two blurred stars as one and a wide one showing them clearly as two.
explanations.context: This card adds sharpness and magnifying to what you learned about telescopes collecting light.

explanations.concept: Seeing light our eyes cannot see
explanations.definition: Light comes in many kinds. Our eyes see only a narrow band. Radio waves, infrared, ultraviolet and X-rays are also light, and different telescopes catch them.
explanations.description: The air blocks most X-rays and ultraviolet light, and part of the infrared. So telescopes for those kinds of light must go above the air. India's AstroSat, launched in 2015, studies the sky in ultraviolet and X-rays. Radio waves pass through air and clouds easily. So radio telescopes can stand on the ground. The Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope at Khodad near Pune has 30 dishes, each 45 metres wide, spread over a field about 25 kilometres across. They work together as if they were one huge telescope. The James Webb Space Telescope looks in infrared, the light that warm things give out. It can see through some dust clouds and catch light from the earliest galaxies. It sits about 1.5 million kilometres from the Earth, behind a sunshield about the size of a tennis court, to stay very cold.
examples: A TV remote control sends infrared light that your eyes cannot see, but a phone camera often can.
Radio dishes need no dark sky, so astronomers can use them in the daytime.
A hot cup of tea glows in an infrared camera, though it looks plain in ordinary light.
In 1967 Jocelyn Bell, a student in England, noticed a strange regular beat on the chart of a radio telescope. It was a pulsar, a spinning star, and she was the first to notice it.
explanations.art: A rainbow strip with radio waves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet and X-rays labelled, and a small telescope for each kind.
explanations.context: This card is about telescopes that catch kinds of light that we cannot see.

explanations.concept: Light takes time: looking far is looking back
explanations.definition: Light travels about 300,000 kilometres every second. A light-second is the distance light covers in one second.
explanations.description: Light from the Moon takes about 1.3 seconds to reach us. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds. A radio message to Mars takes between 3 and 22 minutes, depending on where the planets are. Voyager 1, launched in 1977 and now in the space between the stars, is so far that a message takes close to a whole day to reach it. The nearest star after the Sun is a little over 4 light-years away, so the light we see from it left more than 4 years ago. When a telescope looks at a faraway galaxy, it sees light that left billions of years ago. Looking far away is looking back in time.
examples: If the Sun vanished, we would see it go dark only 8 minutes and 20 seconds later.
Controllers of Voyager 1 send a command and wait about two days for the answer to come back.
The light from the Moon you see tonight left it a little over a second ago.
explanations.art: A line from the Earth with marks for the Moon at 1.3 seconds, the Sun at 8 minutes, Mars at up to 22 minutes and Voyager 1 at about a day.
explanations.context: This card is about how long light and radio signals take to cross space.

explanations.concept: What space does to a body
explanations.definition: In weightlessness, an astronaut's bones and muscles get weaker because they no longer carry the body's weight. Space radiation also adds a risk to health.
explanations.description: On Earth, your legs and back work against gravity all day, and that keeps them strong. In orbit there is no weight to carry. Astronauts lose bone, roughly one percent each month in the bones of the hips and legs, and their muscles shrink. Body fluids move up towards the head, which makes faces puffy and can change eyesight. To fight this, astronauts on the space station exercise about two hours every day on a treadmill and other machines. The station is inside the Earth's magnetic field, which turns away much of the radiation. A trip to the Moon or Mars goes beyond that shelter. Peggy Whitson spent more than 600 days in space in all, and showed that a body can manage long stays with the right exercise.
examples: After months in orbit, an astronaut may find it hard to stand at first when she returns to Earth.
Astronauts strap themselves onto a treadmill with elastic cords, to push their feet against something.
A metal wall or a water tank around a sleeping place gives extra cover from radiation.
explanations.art: An astronaut running on a treadmill fixed to the wall of the space station, with elastic cords holding her down.
explanations.context: This card is about how a body changes in space and how astronauts protect themselves.

explanations.definition: Space junk is the broken and unused things that still orbit the Earth. At orbital speed even a tiny piece can do great damage.
explanations.description: Since 1957, thousands of rockets and satellites have been launched. Dead satellites, empty rocket stages and the pieces from collisions still orbit the Earth. Tens of thousands of pieces bigger than about 10 centimetres are tracked, and there are millions of smaller flecks. Something moving at 8 kilometres a second carries more energy than a bullet, even if it is only a fleck of paint. In 2009, a working satellite and a dead one collided and made thousands of pieces. The space station has moved out of the way of junk several times. Junk in low orbits slowly falls back, because there is a trace of air even at that height, and it burns up. Junk at 36,000 kilometres stays for ages. So old satellites there are pushed a little higher, into a 'graveyard' orbit, before they die.
examples: A speck of paint has cracked a window of the space station.
The Moon's orbit has no air to clean it, so junk there would stay.
Future satellites may carry a way to drop out of orbit when their job is done.
explanations.art: A swarm of tiny dots round the Earth, a satellite with a cracked panel, and an arrow showing a dead satellite being pushed into a higher graveyard orbit.
explanations.context: This card is about the broken things left in orbit and why they are a danger.

explanations.concept: Could people ever reach another star?
explanations.description: The nearest star after the Sun is Proxima Centauri, a little over 4 light-years away. Voyager 1 moves at about 17 kilometres a second, which is about 17,000 times slower than light. At that speed it would take about 70,000 years. No rocket we can build now could do much better. Scientists have ideas, but none has been built.
examples: A light sail is a thin mirror pushed by light itself, with no fuel. A project announced in 2016 imagined pushing tiny chips this way with powerful lasers.
A generation ship would carry people who live and die on the journey, so that their great-grandchildren arrive.

perspectives.explanation: Tiny probes pushed by light may reach another star in a few decades, but people could not go this way.
A ship big enough for people would need amounts of energy that nobody knows how to make. They think the stars are for telescopes, not for travel.

explanations.art: A tiny chip with a huge shiny sail leaving the solar system, with a faraway star ahead.
explanations.context: This card is about whether people could ever visit another star. It is still an idea, with no answer yet.

explanations.concept: Who owns the Moon and the planets?
explanations.description: In 1967, countries including India signed the Outer Space Treaty. It says that no country can claim the Moon or any planet, and that space should be used for peaceful purposes. But it does not clearly say who may own things dug up from the Moon or from asteroids. In 2015 the United States passed a law letting its companies keep resources they take from space. Luxembourg, Japan and some other countries passed similar laws later.
examples: A company that digs up Moon ice for water could be allowed to sell it, under some national laws.
Antarctica is shared by many countries under a treaty and has no owner. Some people think the Moon should be like that.

perspectives.explanation: Companies will not pay for expensive missions unless they can keep what they find. Without rights, nobody will go.
The Moon belongs to all humankind. A few rich countries or companies should not take its best places and its resources.
The old treaty is too vague. The world needs new agreements, made before the first mine is dug.

explanations.art: The Moon with a flag of every colour on it, and a lawyer and an engineer on either side pointing at it.
explanations.context: This card is about a real argument: who, if anyone, may own things in space.

explanations.concept: India's way: small steps and learning from mistakes
explanations.definition: India's space agency, ISRO, builds each mission as a careful step beyond the last, and learns from failures.
explanations.description: In 2014, India's Mangalyaan reached Mars orbit on the first try. No other country had done that. It was reported to cost about 450 crore rupees, much less than most Mars missions. Ritu Karidhal, an engineer from Lucknow, was among the team leaders. In September 2019, the lander of Chandrayaan-2 lost contact just before touching down. The orbiter stayed in good health and kept working around the Moon for years. ISRO studied what went wrong, changed the lander and its landing plan, and tried again. Chandrayaan-3 landed on 23 August 2023. Its project director was P. Veeramuthuvel, from Tamil Nadu. India was the fourth country to land on the Moon, and the first near its south pole.
examples: Chandrayaan-3 reused the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter, which was still working, to talk to the lander.
Engineers chose a bigger landing area, so that a small error would not matter.
Many of the engineers and scientists at ISRO are women, and several led teams in these missions.
explanations.art: A team in a control room with a screen showing a lander near the Moon and a hand writing 'What went wrong?' on a board.
explanations.context: This card is about how ISRO tries again after a failed landing and reaches the Moon's south pole.

agreed.text: An orbit is a fall that keeps missing. A satellite in orbit is in free fall.
agreed.evidence: The crew of the space station float beside everything, as in any fall. Newton's maths of falling and sideways speed predicts the paths of thousands of satellites.

agreed.text: The lower a satellite orbits, the faster it moves and the shorter its lap.
agreed.evidence: Radar and laser tracking give the heights and lap times of satellites, and they follow this rule from 90 minutes at 400 kilometres to 24 hours at 36,000 kilometres.

agreed.text: A rocket's final speed depends on how fast its gas leaves and on how much of its weight is propellant.
agreed.evidence: Every rocket launched fits this rule. In the balloon test, adding weight to the same balloon always shortened the distance.

agreed.text: A wider telescope opening collects more light and shows finer detail.
agreed.evidence: Each time bigger mirrors have been built, astronomers have seen fainter things and split stars that looked single.

agreed.text: Light travels at the same speed everywhere, about 300,000 kilometres a second.
agreed.evidence: Laser flashes bounced off mirrors left on the Moon by astronauts and by a Soviet rover return after about 2.6 seconds, and the Moon's distance can be measured this way to a few centimetres.

agreed.text: Radio waves pass through clouds, but the air blocks most X-rays and ultraviolet light.
agreed.evidence: Radio telescopes work on cloudy days. X-ray telescopes see almost nothing from the ground and work well in orbit.

agreed.text: Weightlessness weakens bones and muscles, and exercise slows the loss.
agreed.evidence: Hundreds of astronauts have been measured before, during and after their stays on space stations.

challenging.claim: Satellites stay up because they are so high that Earth's gravity cannot reach them.
challenging.who: A very common idea, even among grown-ups
challenging.for: Astronauts float, and things seem to weigh nothing up there.
challenging.against: At the height of the space station, gravity is still about nine tenths as strong as on the ground. The station would fall straight back if it stopped moving sideways. Gravity is what bends its path into a circle.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that satellites are beyond the reach of gravity.

challenging.claim: To reach orbit, a rocket just has to go high enough.
challenging.who: Many people before they learn about orbits
challenging.for: A rocket does go up, and space is up.
challenging.against: A rocket that reached 400 kilometres and then stopped would fall straight back down. What keeps a satellite up is its sideways speed of about 8 kilometres a second, which takes most of the rocket's effort.
challenging.context: This card is about what a rocket really has to do to reach orbit.

challenging.claim: A strong telescope on the Earth can see the flag that astronauts left on the Moon.
challenging.for: Telescopes show craters on the Moon, and a flag seems like a small step down from a crater.
challenging.against: The flag is about a metre wide. The Moon is 384,000 kilometres away. The finest detail even the Hubble Space Telescope can show is far bigger than a flag. The landing sites have been photographed by spacecraft that circle the Moon low down.
challenging.context: This card is about what a telescope can and cannot show on the Moon.

challenging.claim: Space is freezing cold everywhere, so anything left there freezes at once.
challenging.for: Space is mostly empty and dark, and the shadows on the Moon are extremely cold.
challenging.against: Empty space has almost no matter to carry heat. A surface in sunlight on the space station can reach well over 100 degrees Celsius, and the shaded side can fall below minus 100. Spacecraft need both heaters and ways to shed heat.
challenging.context: This card is about the temperature of space, which depends on whether the Sun is shining on a thing.

challenging.claim: The Apollo Moon landings were faked in a studio.
challenging.for: The photographs have odd shadows and no stars, and the flag seems to wave.
challenging.against: Cameras set for bright ground cannot show faint stars. The flag had a rod across the top, and it moved only when touched. About 380 kilograms of rock came back and has been studied by labs in many countries. The Soviet Union, a rival that tracked the flights, never said they were fake. Mirrors the astronauts left on the Moon still bounce lasers back today.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous claim that the Moon landings never happened, and the evidence against it.

challenging.claim: Space is so big that space junk is nothing to worry about.
challenging.who: Some people, and some companies in the past
challenging.for: Space has a huge volume, and most satellites have never been hit.
challenging.against: Satellites use a few popular orbits, so the junk is crowded in a thin region near the Earth. A collision in 2009 produced thousands of pieces. More satellites are launched every year, and each collision makes more junk.
challenging.context: This card is about a real argument: is space junk a real problem, or an exaggerated one?

big_questions.q: A satellite is falling all the time and never lands. Is it falling, or is it flying?
big_questions.hint: Think about the marble in the test: while it was in the air, what was gravity doing to it?

big_questions.q: Gravity still pulls on an astronaut in orbit, yet she feels no weight. What do we really mean by feeling weight?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you feel when you stand on the floor. Is it gravity, or the floor pushing back?

big_questions.q: A message to Voyager 1 takes close to a day to arrive. In what sense is Voyager 'there' while we are talking to it?

big_questions.q: Hubble sees galaxies as they were billions of years ago. Is a telescope also a clock that looks backward?

big_questions.q: Space junk comes from our own rockets. Who should clean it up, and who should pay?
big_questions.hint: Think about who launched what, and who is harmed if a satellite fails.

big_questions.q: The Moon belongs to no country by law. Should anything on the Moon belong to anybody?
big_questions.hint: Think about the air, the sea and Antarctica, and how people have shared them or failed to.

big_questions.q: Astronauts often say that seeing the whole Earth from space changed how they felt about it. Why would a view from far away change what someone cares about?

big_questions.q: The Moon also falls around the Earth and keeps missing. Is the whole Earth falling too?

story.title: The Stone That Missed the Sea
story.note: Thamarai, her aunt Chithi and the village are made up. The science is real. A ship does vanish hull first beyond the horizon. India does have a rocket engine testing centre at Mahendragiri in Tirunelveli district. Fisher families in India are given small satellite alert devices, and weather offices send them warnings about the sea. The details of this rescue are imagined.
text: The sea at Kanyakumari was turning from blue to copper. Thamarai sat on a rock with her feet in the foam. She was nine, and she was watching her father's boat go out to fish, as she did every evening.
The boat grew smaller and smaller. Then something odd happened. The bottom of the boat disappeared first. The sail stayed for a moment. Then the sail went too.
"Chithi," she said, "the sea is eating the boat. Why does the bottom go first?"
Her aunt sat down beside her. Chithi was an engineer who tested rocket engines at Mahendragiri, and she was home for the holidays. She picked up a small stone.
"Throw this," she said. "As far as you can into the sea."
Thamarai threw. The stone made a curve and went splash, a short way out.
"Again, harder," said Chithi.
Thamarai threw harder. The splash was farther. She threw with all her strength, and it was farther still.
"Now think," said Chithi. "What does the stone do the whole time it is in the air?"
"It falls," said Thamarai. "From the moment it leaves my hand."
"Good. So every throw is a fall. A harder throw is a fall that lands farther away. Now, if you were as strong as a cannon, how far could you throw?"
"Very far. But not forever."

"The sea is not flat," said Chithi. "It is a piece of a very big ball. Look at your father's boat. The ball of the Earth curves down between your eyes and the boat. First the bottom is hidden behind the curve, and then the sail. The ground bends away from you."
Thamarai looked at the horizon. For the first time, she saw it as the edge of a curve.
"So if I threw the stone fast enough," she said slowly, "the sea would bend away just as the stone fell."

"Yes," said Chithi. "And the stone would fall all the time, and never reach the water. It would go all the way round. That is how a satellite stays up. It does not hang there. It falls, and the Earth curves away, and so it keeps missing. It needs about eight kilometres every second. Nobody can throw like that. A rocket does the throwing."
"That is what you do at Mahendragiri?"
"I test the engines that make the throw," said Chithi, smiling. "A rocket spends only a short time going up. Then it tips over and spends most of its fuel going sideways."
The sky went dark. A few stars came out. Thamarai noticed that her father's boat had no lamp she could see.
"Chithi, he is late."
A man ran down the beach, waving his phone. "There is a storm warning! The weather office says the wind is rising. All the boats must come in!"
The women of the village gathered at the shore. The wind began to tug at Thamarai's hair. Waves came higher up the rocks.
Then Thamarai's mother held up a small orange box. "This is the alert box the fisheries office gave to every boat. Your father has one. If he is in trouble, he presses the button."
"How does the box talk?" asked Thamarai. "There are no towers in the sea."

"It talks to a satellite," said Chithi. She was looking at the sky. "A very special one. It is 36,000 kilometres up, over the equator. At that height, one lap round the Earth takes exactly one day. The Earth turns once a day too. So the satellite hangs above the same spot in the sky all the time, like a lamp on a hook. The box always knows where to point."

A phone buzzed in Thamarai's mother's hand. She read the message and let out a long breath. "The coast guard has his position. The boat's engine failed, but he is safe, drifting about ten kilometres out. A coast guard boat is on its way."
Everyone cheered. Thamarai felt her knees go weak and she sat down on the sand.
Two hours later, the lights of a big ship came in, with her father's small boat behind it on a rope. He stepped onto the beach, wet and tired and smiling.

That night Thamarai lay on the roof and looked at the stars. She knew now that one of them was not a star at all. It was a box of metal 36,000 kilometres away, falling round the Earth and always missing, and moving so exactly in time with the turning of the world that it stayed above her village.

She took a pebble from her pocket. She held it out over the dark sea and opened her hand. It fell, as it always had. Now she knew why. The pebble had no sideways speed, so it landed. A satellite has so much that it never does.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a satellite is not held up by anything. It is falling around the Earth and missing. A higher orbit is slower, and at 36,000 kilometres one lap takes exactly one day. That matches the Earth's spin, so the satellite stays over the same spot. That is why the alert box could always point to one place in the sky.

What would you have to do to a thrown stone so that it never landed in the sea?
Why can a satellite 36,000 kilometres up stay above one spot of the ground all the time?
Chithi said a rocket spends most of its fuel going sideways. Why?
Why did the pebble land in the sea, when a satellite never lands?

roots.context: We rolled marbles, loaded a rocket and followed satellites round the Earth. Now we ask what falling, orbits and distance tell us about the world we live in.

deep_truth.truth: In the marble test, faster marbles landed farther away. A marble fast enough to miss the whole floor would never land. A satellite is exactly that, always falling and always missing. So staying up and falling turn out to be one motion.
deep_truth.habit: We picture staying up as being held up, like a lamp on a hook. We think falling is the opposite of staying up. A satellite shows that one motion can be both.
deep_truth.evidence: In Falling Sideways, every marble spent about the same time in the air, but the faster ones landed farther along. The Earth's ground curves away by about 5 metres over 8 kilometres, and the space station moves 8 kilometres every second. If your own marbles landed differently, write down exactly what they did and test again.

three.who_am_i: You are standing on a planet that is falling around the Sun all the time. You ride along without feeling a thing, as an astronaut rides along with her station.
three.what_is_life: Our bones and muscles are built for working against gravity. Take away the load and they shrink within weeks. A living body keeps its shape by using it.
three.what_is_this_world: A thrown stone, the Moon and the space station follow one rule of falling, and differ only in their sideways speed.

roots.thread: A dropped marble, the Moon and the space station are all falling, and the only difference is how fast they move sideways. A slow throw lands near. A faster throw lands far. A throw of about 8 kilometres a second misses the Earth for ever. So 'up there' is not a place where the rules stop. The same gravity that pulls a pebble out of your hand also holds the Moon in its path and the Earth in its path round the Sun.

teachings.teaching: An ancient hymn asks who really knows how the world began and where it all came from. It ends by saying that perhaps the one who watches from the highest heaven knows, or perhaps even that one does not.
teachings.link: The farther we look, the older the light we see. A telescope shows us how far our knowing goes, and the hymn reminds us to say where it stops.

teachings.teaching: Many astronauts who have seen the whole Earth from orbit say that it changed how they felt. They saw one round world with no lines between countries and a very thin layer of air. Frank White gave this feeling the name 'the overview effect'.
teachings.link: From far enough away, the thin skin of air you measured on your lime becomes plain to see. A far view can show something that is hard to notice from the ground.

science.text: A satellite in orbit is in free fall around the Earth, and the same gravity holds the Moon and the planets in their paths.
Seeing the whole Earth from space changes how many astronauts feel. Researchers are still working out how common this is and why it happens.

other_view.view: 'Falling' and 'flying' are only words. What matters is the path, and the path comes from a few numbers: the speed, the height and the pull of the Earth. Asking whether a satellite is 'really' falling adds nothing to the maths.

practice.title: Feel the floor push up
practice.say: Stand with your feet apart and close your eyes. Feel the floor pushing up on the soles of your feet. That push is what you call your weight. Now imagine the floor is gone and you are falling, and the push is gone too. That is how an astronaut feels. Breathe in slowly three times. Then open your eyes and feel the floor again.
practice.kid: Stand still. Close your eyes. Feel the floor push up on your feet. Imagine it gone. Breathe slowly three times.

ask: If you were falling for ever and the ground kept curving away, would you feel like you were falling?
The Earth is falling round the Sun, and you feel nothing. What else might be moving that we do not notice?
From far away the Earth looks like one round world. What would you notice about it that you cannot notice from the ground?
roots.art: A child standing with eyes closed and a faint picture behind her of the Earth falling round the Sun, with the space station and the Moon on their own circles.

games.title: A, B or Same: which one is faster, longer or stronger?
games.context: This is a card game. Each card compares two things from space. Players guess whether A, B or neither is bigger or faster, and then give the reason.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a pile in the middle of a table, with three tokens in front of each player: A, B and Same.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while the other players each put a token face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone else picks a token.

setup.art: All the tokens turned over together, and the reader reading the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader reads the answer.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: a comparison on the front, and the answer with the reason on the back

items.f: A: the space station, 400 km up. B: a satellite 36,000 km up. Which one takes longer to go round the Earth once?
items.b: B. Higher satellites are slower. One lap takes 24 hours there and about 90 minutes for the station.

items.f: A: a satellite at 36,000 km. B: the Moon. Which one moves faster?
items.b: A. Closer orbits are faster. The satellite moves at about 3 km a second and the Moon at about 1.

items.f: A: a balloon rocket with no paper clips. B: the same rocket with 10 clips. Which one goes farther?
items.b: A. The same push moves a lighter rocket farther.

items.f: A: the propellant in a big rocket at lift-off. B: the satellite on top. Which weighs more?
items.b: A. Around nine tenths of the weight at lift-off is propellant. The satellite is only a few percent.

items.f: A: sunlight reaching the Earth. B: moonlight reaching the Earth. Which light left its source more recently?
items.b: B. Moonlight left the Moon about 1.3 seconds ago. Sunlight left the Sun about 8 minutes ago.

items.f: A: a telescope mirror 1 metre wide. B: a mirror 2 metres wide. Which shows finer detail?
items.b: B. A wider opening collects more light and shows finer detail.

items.f: A: radio waves from space. B: X-rays from space. Which easily reach a telescope on the ground?
items.b: A. The air lets radio waves through and blocks most X-rays.

items.f: A: a telescope in a big city under bright lights. B: a telescope at Hanle in Ladakh, high, dry and dark. Which gets the darker, steadier sky?
items.b: B. Less air above it, little cloud and almost no city light make a better sky.

items.f: A: an astronaut after six months in orbit with no exercise. B: a person after six months at home. Whose leg bones are weaker?
items.b: A. Without weight to carry, bones lose strength.

items.f: A: a fleck of paint at 8 km a second. B: a cricket ball at 30 metres a second. Which carries more energy for each gram?
items.b: A. Energy grows very fast with speed. The fleck is about 270 times faster.

items.f: A: a marble rolled off a table fast. B: a marble dropped from the table's edge at the same moment. Which one hits the floor first?
items.b: Same. Sideways speed does not change how long the fall takes.

items.f: A: Chandrayaan-3's 40-day trip in many small burns. B: a direct push to the Moon in about 3 days. Which one needs the bigger rocket?
items.b: B. Many small burns trade time for rocket size.

items.f: A: a rocket's effort in climbing up through thick air. B: its effort in gaining sideways speed. Which is bigger?
items.b: B. Staying up needs about 8 km a second sideways. Climbing 400 km needs only about a third of that.

items.f: A: a hammer and B: a feather dropped together on the Moon, where there is no air. Which one lands first?
items.b: Same. With no air to slow the feather, both fall alike. An astronaut showed this in 1971.

items.f: A: a radio message to Mars at the closest. B: sunlight travelling to the Earth. Which one takes longer?
items.b: B. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds. The message takes about 3 minutes at best.

items.f: A: one radio dish alone. B: the 30 dishes of the GMRT working together. Which can show finer detail?
items.b: B. Dishes spread far apart act like one huge telescope.

items.f: A: an infrared telescope on a hot, humid plain. B: the same telescope in space. Which one catches more clean infrared light?
items.b: B. The air blocks part of the infrared and glows warm itself.

items.f: A: gravity on the Moon's surface. B: gravity at the height of the space station. Which is stronger?
items.b: B. The station is only 400 km up, so gravity is about nine tenths of that on the ground. On the Moon it is about one sixth.

items.f: A: a TV dish aimed at a geostationary satellite. B: a dish aimed at the space station. Which one must keep turning to follow?
items.b: B. The station moves across the sky. The geostationary satellite stays above one spot.

items.f: A: a magnifying glass 5 cm wide. B: one 10 cm wide. Which gathers about 4 times as much light?
items.b: B. Twice as wide means four times the area.

items.f: A: a rocket that drops its empty stage. B: a rocket that keeps it. Which reaches the higher speed with the same fuel?
items.b: A. Dead weight dropped makes the rest easier to push.

items.f: A: Earth's pull on you on the ground. B: Earth's pull on you on the space station. Which is bigger?
items.b: A. It is a little weaker at 400 km up, but still about nine tenths.

items.f: A: an old satellite left at 36,000 km. B: a broken satellite left at 400 km. Which one stays up longer?
items.b: A. At 400 km a trace of air slows it, and it falls and burns up. At 36,000 km it can stay for ages.

items.f: A: a cannonball fired at 2 km a second from a very high mountain. B: one fired at 8 km a second. Which one goes right round the Earth?
items.b: B. At about 8 km a second the ground curves away as fast as the ball falls.

printables.title: 12 tokens: four that say A, four that say B and four that say Same

rules: One player is the reader. The reader shuffles the cards and takes the top one. Every other player takes one A token, one B token and one Same token.
The reader reads the front of a card aloud and does not show the back.
Every other player puts one token face down. Then everyone turns their tokens over together.
The reader reads the back aloud. A player who chose right scores 1 point.
A player who also gives the reason in their own words scores 1 more point. The reader checks it against the back.
After each card, the job of reader passes to the next player. Keep going until the cards are used up, or one player has 10 points.
With only two people, one reads and the other plays, then you swap after every card. Playing alone, read the front, say your answer and reason out loud, then turn the card over.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the 12 tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile. Give each player one A, one B and one Same token.
flow.say: Each card compares two things from space. You choose A, B or Same. Then we find out who was right and why.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take an A, a B and a Same.
flow.context: This is the first step of the A, B or Same card game. You set up the cards and tokens.

flow.do: Play the first eight cards. After each card, read the back and ask for a reason. After the third card, ask the question below.
flow.say: I read the front. Choose a token. Turn them over together. Now the back says the answer. Who can say why in their own words?
flow.kid: The reader reads. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: Which cards so far were about slower or faster, and what rule decided them?
good: Higher orbits are slower.
More weight means less speed from the same push.
Closer to the Earth is faster.

flow.context: In this step you play the first cards and learn how to score.

flow.do: Play the rest of the cards. Swap the reader after each card. Keep a score on paper.
flow.say: Next card. Make a guess first. Do not look at the back. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Keep playing. Swap the reader each time. Write down your points.
flow.parent: If a child picks the wrong one, read the reason and ask them to say it back in their own words. That counts as learning, not losing.

flow.do: Count the points. Talk about the card that nearly fooled everyone.
flow.say: Which card fooled you most? What did you think, and what is the real reason?
flow.kid: Which card fooled you? Why?

check.q: A marble is rolled off a table and another is dropped from the edge at the same moment. Which lands first?
options: The rolled one, because it is faster
The dropped one, because it goes straight down
They land together
check.why: Sideways speed does not change the fall. Both marbles fall the same height with the same pull, so they take the same time. The rolled one just lands farther away.

games.title: Mission Chain: put the 40 days of Chandrayaan-3 in order
games.context: This game puts the steps of a real mission in the right order. Players take turns placing one card at a time and say why that step has to come next.

setup.art: Twelve cards in a jumble on the floor, each with a small picture of a step: a rocket, an oval orbit, a Moon orbit, a lander and a rover.
setup.caption: 1. Spread the twelve cards face up in a jumble.

setup.art: A child placing a card at the start of a line, with the next place left empty.
setup.caption: 2. Take turns putting the next card in the line.

printables.title: 12 two-sided cards: a step on the front, and its number with a clue on the back

items.f: The rocket lifts off from Sriharikota with the spacecraft on top.
items.b: Step 1. Everything starts with the launch, on 14 July 2023.

items.f: The rocket leaves the spacecraft in a long oval orbit round the Earth.
items.b: Step 2. The spacecraft is now in orbit but still near the Earth.

items.f: The spacecraft's engine burns near the closest point to the Earth, again and again.
items.b: Step 3. Each burn stretches the oval farther out from the Earth.

items.f: A last burn sends the spacecraft off towards the Moon, on 1 August.
items.b: Step 4. It now leaves the Earth's orbit and heads for the Moon.

items.f: The Moon's gravity catches the spacecraft, on 5 August, and it starts to orbit the Moon.
items.b: Step 5. It must slow down a little to be caught by the Moon.

items.f: More burns lower the orbit, step by step, until it is a circle close to the Moon.
items.b: Step 6. A low circle is the starting point for a landing.

items.f: The lander Vikram separates from the part that stays in orbit.
items.b: Step 7. The lander goes down. The rest stays up to talk to it.

items.f: Vikram lowers its orbit again, to bring itself close to the surface.
items.b: Step 8. It gets close before the final descent.

items.f: Vikram fires its engines to slow down and comes down gently near the south pole, on 23 August.
items.b: Step 9. The landing happens only after the lander is low and slow.

items.f: The rover Pragyan rolls down the ramp onto the Moon's dust.
items.b: Step 10. The rover can leave only after the lander has landed.

items.f: The lander and rover measure the ground and the dust for one Moon day, about 14 Earth days.
items.b: Step 11. Sunlight powers the work.

items.f: Night falls on the Moon for about 14 Earth days, and the machines go to sleep.
items.b: Step 12. Without sunlight the solar-powered machines stop.

printables.title: Score sheet
items: Reasons given in your own words

rules: Spread all 12 cards face up in a jumble, with the step side showing. Do not turn them over.
On your turn, pick the card that you think comes next in the line, and put it at the end of the line.
Say in your own words why this step has to come after the one before it.
Turn the card over and read its step number. If you were right, it stays and you score 1 point. If you gave a good reason, you score 1 more.
If you were wrong, put the card back in the jumble. The next player has a turn.
When all 12 cards are in the line, the player with the most points wins. If two players have the same score, they win together.
Playing alone, order all 12 cards, then turn them over and count how many you placed right.

flow.do: Cut out the 12 cards. Spread them face up in a jumble. Read each step out loud once.
flow.say: These twelve cards are the steps of a real journey to the Moon. We will put them in order. First, let me read each one.
flow.kid: Read all the cards once. Spread them out.
flow.context: This is the first step of Mission Chain, a game about the 40 days it took Chandrayaan-3 to reach the Moon.

flow.do: Take turns placing the next card. Check the back after each one. Ask for the reason every time.
flow.say: Which card comes next? Why does it have to come after that one? Now turn it over and check.
flow.kid: Pick the next card. Say why. Turn it over.
flow.parent: The hard part is steps 3 to 6. They are all about burns that make the orbit bigger, then lower. Ask: before the Moon catches it, what must happen? After it is caught, what must happen before a landing?

check.q: Why does the spacecraft make several small burns around the Earth, and not one big push to the Moon?
options: A single big push needs a much bigger rocket
The spacecraft is waiting for the Moon to rise
It is checking the weather
check.why: A rocket that can lift the spacecraft only to a low orbit cannot throw it all the way to the Moon at once. The spacecraft's own small engine does the rest in many burns. This trades time for rocket size.

flow.do: Look at the finished line. Count the days from step 1 to step 9.
flow.say: From 14 July to 23 August is 40 days. Which steps took the most days? Which took only minutes?
flow.kid: Count the days from launch to landing. Which part took longest?
flow.parent: Most of the 40 days went on raising the orbit round the Earth and then lowering it round the Moon. The final landing took only minutes.

experiments.title: Falling Sideways: does a faster marble take longer to land?
experiments.question: A marble rolls off the edge of a table. If it leaves the table faster, does it land farther away? And does it take longer to reach the floor?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will a faster marble land farther away, in the same place, or nearer? Will it take longer to fall? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same marble, the same ramp and the same table every time. Only the height that you let the marble go from changes: 5, 10 and 15 centimetres above the table top. Let go of the marble without pushing it. Roll it three times from each height, and use the middle landing mark, because one try can be a fluke.
results_table: My guess for the landing distance (cm)

materials.item: a marble or a small steel ball, about 1.5 centimetres across
a plastic ruler with a groove down the middle, 30 centimetres long, or a stiff strip of card folded into a channel
a table at least 70 centimetres high with a smooth, square edge, and a floor that is not carpet
3 or 4 books, to hold up the high end of the ramp
4 sheets of newspaper, laid end to end along the floor from under the table edge
a saucer with a little water in it, to wet the marble so that it leaves a clear spot (add a pinch of haldi or a drop of ink to the water)
a second marble (or a small ball of clay) for the two-marble race, a measuring tape, a pencil and masking tape

experiments.safety: Keep marbles away from children under five, who might put them in their mouths. Wipe up any water that drips on the floor, so nobody slips. Pick up stray marbles at once, because stepping on one can make you fall. Haldi stains cloth, so keep the saucer off carpets.

schedule.what: Set up the ramp. Roll the marble from three heights, three times each. Measure the landing marks. Race two marbles off the edge and listen. Think about what speed a marble would need to miss a round floor.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw three bars, one for each start height, as long as its middle landing distance. Write one sentence under the bars that says what the pattern is.

flow.do: Show your child the marble, the ramp and the newspaper on the floor. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write down the guess.
flow.say: A marble will roll off the edge of the table. Does a faster marble land farther away? Does it take longer to fall? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A marble rolls off a table. If it is faster, where does it land? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the faster marble will land there?
good: It has more speed, so it flies farther.
It stays in the air longer.
It lands in the same place because gravity is the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say a faster marble takes longer in the air. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of Falling Sideways. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Lay the ruler so its low end rests on the table, 15 centimetres from the edge. Stack books under the other end. Tape a line on the newspaper right under the table edge. This is the zero line.
flow.say: The ruler is a ramp. The higher the marble starts, the faster it will be at the bottom. The tape under the edge is zero. We measure from there.
flow.kid: Make a ramp. Tape a zero line on the floor under the table edge.
flow.parent: The marble runs off the low end, across 15 centimetres of flat table, and over the edge. Use a ruler with a groove so the marble goes straight. Raise the high end so that the marble starts 5 centimetres above the table. Mark 5, 10 and 15 centimetres on a pencil line on the books if you wish.

check.q: Why does the marble start from the same ramp each time and change only its starting height?
options: So only the speed changes and every other thing stays the same
So the marble does not get lost
So the ramp is easier to build
check.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. If the ramp, marble and table all stayed the same, any change in where the marble lands must come from its speed.

flow.context: In this step you build the ramp and mark the zero line on the floor.

flow.do: Dip the marble in the water and shake it once. Let it go from the 5 centimetre mark. Look for the wet spot nearest to the table. Mark it with a pencil dot. Measure from the zero line. Do it three times, then at 10 and at 15 centimetres.
flow.say: Let the marble go. Do not push it. Watch where it first touches the paper. Mark the first wet spot only. It may bounce on after that.
flow.kid: Wet the marble. Let it go. Mark the first spot. Measure from zero.
flow.parent: A grown-up can watch the landing, because it is hard to roll and watch at the same time. The marble may bounce. Only the first wet spot counts. Alone, the child lets go and the grown-up watches the landing. With 2 to 4 children: one lets go, one watches and marks the spot, one measures, one writes; swap after each height. Typical landings are roughly 30 to 80 centimetres from the edge, but your numbers will differ. If a try goes very differently from the other two, repeat it. If the wet spots are too faint, wet the marble more or use a dry newspaper under a dark pen dot. Your numbers will differ from the example. What matters is that the higher start lands farther.
flow.context: In this step you roll the marble from three heights and measure where it first lands.

flow.do: Find the middle number for each height. Draw the three bars. Look at how the distance grew when the start height grew. Then the two-marble race: put two marbles side by side at the table edge. A partner flicks one off sideways, hard, while you let the other just slide off at the same moment. Listen for one click or two. Do it five times.
flow.say: Look at our numbers. Which start height gave the farthest landing? Did the landing double when the height doubled?
flow.kid: Which height landed farthest? Draw a bar for each one.
flow.parent: The distance grows with the speed, but not in step with the height. Doubling the height does not double the distance. The marble's speed grows more slowly than the height does. Do not explain this yet. Just notice. In the race, most clean tries sound like one click, because both marbles fall the same height in the same time. Two clicks usually mean one marble was let go late, so repeat and count only the clean tries.

check.q: The marble that started higher left the table faster. Where did it land?
options: Farther from the table
Nearer to the table
In the same place
check.why: A faster marble moves sideways farther in the time it takes to fall to the floor. The time to fall is about the same for every marble, but a faster marble covers more ground in that time.

flow.do: Ask for what I think, what I saw and why. Then ask the Earth question.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why? Now imagine the floor curved away downwards. How fast would the marble need to go so that it never landed?
flow.kid: Say what I think, what I saw and why. Then think: a curved floor.
flow.parent: This is claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer: what I think: a faster marble lands farther away. What I saw: the marble from 15 centimetres landed about one and a half times as far as the one from 5, for example. Why: all the marbles fell the same height, so they took about the same time to fall, but the faster ones moved farther sideways in that time. Then the Earth question: on the real Earth the ground curves away by about 5 metres over 8 kilometres. A thing that falls 5 metres in a second and moves 8 kilometres in that second would never reach the ground. That is a satellite. You can say: the marble fell and missed only a little. A satellite falls and misses all the way round.

check.q: A cannonball is fired sideways from a very high mountain. What would make it go right round the Earth and never land?
options: Being fired fast enough, about 8 kilometres a second
Being a heavier cannonball
Being fired a little higher up
check.why: The ground curves away below the ball as it falls. If the ball moves sideways fast enough, the ground drops away as fast as the ball falls, so it keeps missing. A heavier ball falls the same way, so weight does not matter.

experiments.context: In this experiment you roll a marble off a table from three starting heights and measure where it lands. It shows how speed decides how far a falling thing travels, which is the idea behind every satellite.

experiments.title: The Loaded Balloon Rocket: how much does extra weight slow a rocket?
experiments.question: A balloon rocket flies along a string. If you tape paper clips on it, does it still fly as far? How much shorter is the flight for every extra clip?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How far will the rocket go with no clips, with 10 clips and with 20 clips? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same balloon blown up to the same size every time. Check the size with a loop of string that just fits round the fattest part. Use the same string, the same straw and the same starting mark. Only the number of paper clips changes. Fly each load twice. Mark where the front of the straw stops.

materials.item: 4 metres of smooth thread or thin nylon cord
a drinking straw, cut to 15 centimetres long
2 balloons of the same kind, about 25 centimetres long when blown up
cello tape, 6 short pieces
30 small paper clips, each about 1 gram
a loop of string 50 centimetres long, to check the balloon size
two chairs, a measuring tape, a clothes peg (or a partner pinching the neck with fingers) and a pencil

experiments.safety: Children under eight should only blow up balloons with a grown-up near, and a burst balloon is picked up and thrown away at once, because small pieces can choke. Skip this test if anyone at home is allergic to latex. Keep the string at knee height so nobody trips on it.

schedule.what: Set up the string. Fly the balloon with no load, then with 10, 20 and 30 clips, twice each. Compare the distances and think about what this means for a real rocket.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a line graph of distance against the number of clips. Write one sentence that says what the pattern is.

flow.do: Show your child the balloon, the straw and the paper clips. Say that the clips stand for the weight of a rocket's payload. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: This balloon will be a rocket. Clips are the weight it must carry. How far will it fly with none? With 10? With 20? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A balloon rocket carries clips. How far will it fly with more clips? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think more weight will change how far it flies?
good: A heavier rocket is harder to push.
The same air push has to move more.
It will fly just as far because the push is the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write each guess in the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Loaded Balloon Rocket. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Thread the straw on the string. Tie the string between two chairs, 3 metres apart, at knee height, pulled tight. Tape the balloon to the straw. Mark a start line with a peg.
flow.say: The straw slides on the string like a train on a track. The balloon is the engine. We tape it on so that its neck points back along the string.
flow.kid: Thread the straw on the string. Tape the balloon to the straw.
flow.parent: Tape the balloon along its side, not over the neck, so that its neck points straight back. Pinch the neck with a clothes peg when it is full, then take the peg off to launch. The string must be pulled tight, because a sagging string stops the rocket. Practise one flight with no load to check that the straw slides freely.
flow.context: In this step you build the string track and the balloon rocket.

flow.do: Blow up the balloon until the string loop fits round it. Pinch the neck with the peg. Put the straw at the start line. Take off the peg. Mark where the front of the straw stops. Measure from the start line.
flow.say: Blow the balloon up to the same size every time. Count down from three. Let go. Where does the front of the straw stop?
flow.kid: Blow up the balloon to the loop size. Let go. Mark where it stops.
flow.parent: This first flight has no clips. Alone, the child blows and releases while the grown-up marks the stop. With 2 to 4 children: one blows up the balloon, one pinches the neck, one lets go, one marks and measures; swap after each load. Do it twice. If the balloon gets floppy after a few uses, swap in the second one. The distance on the string may be limited by the chair. Then lengthen the string, or count it as 'the whole string'.
flow.context: In this step you fly the rocket with no clips, so you have something to compare with.

flow.do: Tape 10 clips under the straw. Fly the rocket twice. Then fly it with 20 clips and with 30. Measure each flight. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Now we load the rocket. Tape on 10 clips. Same size balloon, same start line. Does it fly as far?
flow.kid: Add 10 clips. Fly it twice. Then 20. Then 30.
flow.parent: Spread the clips evenly under the straw so the rocket does not tip. A typical party balloon carries 10 clips easily, 20 slowly, and may barely move with 30. If the rocket stops moving, that is a real result: write 0 and note it. If it already struggles at 10 clips, use 5, 10 and 15 instead. Your numbers will differ. What matters is the pattern.

check.q: Why must the balloon be blown up to the same size each time?
options: So the push is the same and only the weight changes
So the balloon looks neat
So it makes less noise
check.why: A bigger balloon holds more air and pushes longer. If the size changed, you would not know whether a short flight was caused by the weight or by less air.

flow.do: Find the average of the two tries for each load. Draw the line graph. Look at how the distance changes with each extra clip.
flow.say: Look at our numbers. What happened to the distance when we added clips? Did every 10 clips take away the same amount?
flow.kid: Draw a graph of distance against clips. What do you see?
flow.parent: The distance falls as clips are added. It may fall faster at first or in a steady way. Your own numbers decide. A rocket with no load would go farthest.

flow.do: Ask for what I think, what I saw and why. Then ask the stage question.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why? Now, a real rocket drops its empty tanks on the way up. Why would that help it?
flow.kid: Say what I think, what I saw and why. Why does a rocket drop its empty tanks?
flow.parent: This is claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer: what I think: a heavier rocket goes less far with the same push. What I saw: with 20 clips the rocket flew about half as far as with none, for example. Why: the same air gives the same push, and the push has more weight to move, so it gives less speed. Then the stage question: when a tank is empty it is only dead weight. If it is dropped, the rest of the rocket is lighter, so the same engine gives it more speed.

check.q: Why does a real rocket drop its empty stage as it climbs?
options: The empty stage is dead weight, and dropping it lets the engine speed the rest up more
The empty stage makes too much noise
The stage is needed on the ground
check.why: The balloon test showed that the same push gives less speed to a heavier rocket. A stage with empty tanks adds weight and no push. Dropping it makes the rest lighter, so the next engine can speed it up more.

experiments.context: In this experiment you tape paper clips to a balloon rocket on a string and measure how far it flies. It shows why every kilogram of weight costs a rocket so much fuel, and why rockets are built in stages.
