experiments.title: A Telescope from Two Lenses: how much bigger does it make faraway things?
experiments.question: Two simple lenses lined up on a stick can make a telescope. How many times bigger do they make something far away, and what decides that number?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will a faraway wall look bigger, smaller or the same through two lenses? Will it look the right way up or upside down? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same two lenses and look at the same faraway wall from the same spot every time. Only the gap between the two lenses changes. Try the gap that looks sharpest, then a gap 3 centimetres shorter and a gap 3 centimetres longer. Look at the same patch of wall each time.
results_table: Is the picture sharp, a little blurry or very blurry?
Right way up or upside down?
How many plain bricks or tiles fit across one magnified one?

materials.item: a weak lens for the front: reading glasses for long sight with a plus (+) number of 2.0 to 2.5, which has a focal length of 40 to 50 centimetres (a grandparent's old glasses are fine; minus glasses will not work), or a large weak magnifying glass
a strong small magnifier for the eyepiece, such as a pocket magnifier or a watchmaker's loupe, that makes things about 5 to 10 times bigger
a straight stick or a metre ruler, about 1 metre long (the two lenses sit about 55 centimetres apart)
modelling clay or rubber bands, to hold the lenses upright on the stick
a faraway wall of bricks, tiles or windows, at least 50 metres away, seen from a window or a terrace
a measuring tape, paper and a pencil

experiments.safety: Never point the lenses at the Sun, and never look at the Sun through them. Sunlight through a lens can burn eyes and start a fire. Put the lenses away in a drawer when you finish. Go on a terrace or balcony only with a grown-up.

schedule.what: Look through each lens alone. Mount both on a stick. Slide them until the faraway wall is sharp. Measure the gap and count how many times bigger the wall looks.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the wall as it looks through the telescope and as it looks to your bare eye. Write the gap at which the picture was sharpest, the focal length of each lens, and whether your brick count was close to the front focal length divided by the eyepiece focal length.

flow.do: Show your child the two lenses. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess.
flow.say: These two lenses will make a telescope. Will a faraway wall look bigger or smaller? The right way up, or upside down? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Two lenses make a telescope. What will a faraway wall look like? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the picture will look that way?
good: A telescope makes things bigger.
It might flip the picture.
Lenses bend light, so it might turn upside down.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Remind your child about the magnifying glass that made an upside-down picture of a window.
flow.context: This is the first step of the two-lens telescope. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Look at the faraway wall through each lens alone. Hold the weak lens at arm's length. Hold the strong magnifier close to your eye. Write what each one does. Then find each lens's focal length. Face a far window or a faraway building, never the Sun. Hold the lens up with a sheet of paper behind it. Slide the paper until a small, sharp, upside-down picture appears. Measure from lens to paper.
flow.say: Hold the weak lens far from your eye. What do you see? Now look through the strong magnifier. Which one makes the wall look bigger?
flow.kid: Look through each lens alone. What does each one do?
flow.parent: The weak lens held at arm's length usually gives a blurry or upside-down picture. The strong magnifier close to the eye gives a very blurry wall, because it is made for near things. Neither is a telescope alone. The window picture gives the focal length: expect about 40 to 50 centimetres for the glasses lens and about 3 to 5 centimetres for a pocket magnifier. Do not hold the paper in sunlight from the window.
flow.context: In this step you try each lens on its own, to see what it does before you join them.

flow.do: Use clay to stand the weak lens upright at the far end of the stick. Stand the strong lens at the near end. Hold the stick up to your eye. Slide the weak lens until the wall looks sharp. Measure the gap.
flow.say: Put your eye close to the small lens. Look through both at the wall. Slide the front lens back and forth, very slowly, until the picture is sharp.
flow.kid: Look through both lenses. Slide the front lens slowly until it is sharp.
flow.parent: This takes patience and a steady hand. Alone, the child looks and the grown-up slides the front lens. With 2 to 4 children: one looks, one slides, one holds the stick steady on a chair, one reads the gap; swap every minute. Rest the stick on a chair or a windowsill. The picture will be upside down, with coloured edges, and a bit blurry. That is normal for simple lenses. The gap that gives a sharp picture is about the two focal lengths added together, for example 50 plus 6, so 56 centimetres. If you cannot find a sharp picture, try the other way round, or change which lens is in front.
flow.context: In this step you mount the two lenses on the stick and find the gap that gives a sharp picture.

flow.do: Keep both eyes open. One eye looks through the telescope. The other looks at the wall. Count how many plain bricks fit across one magnified brick. Write the number. Then try the gap 3 centimetres shorter and 3 centimetres longer.
flow.say: Keep both eyes open. Your brain puts the two pictures on top of each other. How many plain bricks fit across one big brick?
flow.kid: Keep both eyes open. Count how many plain bricks fit across one big brick.
flow.parent: It takes a moment for the two pictures to overlap. If it is too hard, count how many bricks you see across a fixed width through the telescope, and how many with the bare eye. The ratio is the magnifying. Typically about 5 to 15 times, depending on your lenses. It should be close to the front focal length divided by the eyepiece focal length, for example 50 divided by 5 is 10. A weak 3x pocket magnifier gives a smaller number, about 6 to 8.

check.q: Each brick looks 8 times wider through your telescope. What does this number tell you?
options: The telescope magnifies 8 times
The wall is 8 metres away
The lens is 8 centimetres wide
check.why: Magnifying is how many times bigger something looks. If 8 plain bricks fit across one magnified brick, the telescope magnifies 8 times.

flow.do: Ask for what I think, what I saw and why. Then ask the question about stars.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why? A big telescope magnifies more than a small one. But stars stay as dots. Why is that?
flow.kid: Say what I think, what I saw and why. Why do stars stay as dots?
flow.parent: This is claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer: what I think: two lenses make a faraway wall look bigger and upside down. What I saw: each brick looked about 8 times wider, for example, and the picture was sharpest at one gap. Why: the front lens makes a small picture of the wall, and the eyepiece magnifies that picture, so it looks bigger. Then stars: a star is so far away that even a huge telescope shows it as a single point. A big telescope does not make a star bigger. It collects more light and splits stars that are close together.

check.q: A front lens bends light to a point 100 centimetres away and the eyepiece bends it to a point 5 centimetres away. About how much does the telescope magnify?
options: 20 times
5 times
105 times
check.why: Magnifying is the front lens's focal length divided by the eyepiece's focal length. 100 divided by 5 is 20. A weaker front lens or a stronger eyepiece magnifies more.

experiments.context: In this experiment you mount two lenses on a stick to make a simple telescope and measure how much bigger it makes a faraway wall. It shows how Galileo's telescope worked, and what magnifying really means.

activities.title: Orbit Map: draw the satellites to scale on the floor

materials.item: 4 sheets of newspaper, taped together into a sheet at least 90 centimetres across
a pencil tied to a piece of string about 50 centimetres long
a 1 metre ruler for the circles, and a tape measure of 4 metres or more (or a string marked at 3.84 metres with the ruler) for the Moon
a marker or crayons in 4 colours
masking tape and small stickers

schedule.what: Draw the Earth and three orbits to scale. Mark the Moon on the floor. See how thin the lowest orbit is, and how far away the highest ones are.

activities.record: Keep the drawing. Label each circle with the name of the satellite and the time it takes for one lap.

flow.do: Tell your child that 1 centimetre on the paper stands for 1,000 kilometres. Ask them to guess how far from the Earth's edge the space station's circle will be.
flow.say: On this map, 1 centimetre is 1,000 kilometres. The Earth will be a circle with a radius of 6 and a half centimetres. How far above its edge do you think the space station circle will be?
flow.kid: 1 centimetre stands for 1,000 kilometres. Guess how far above the Earth the space station is.
flow.parent: Most children guess several centimetres. Do not correct it yet. The Earth's radius is about 6,371 kilometres, so 6.4 centimetres.
flow.context: In this activity you draw the orbits of satellites to scale, to see how far apart they really are.

flow.do: Tape the sheets together. Mark a dot in the middle. Hold the pencil on the string 6.4 centimetres from the dot, and draw a full circle. This is the Earth. Now draw a circle with a radius of 6.8 centimetres. This is the space station.
flow.say: Hold the string tight at the dot and swing the pencil all the way round. That is the Earth. Now make the string a little longer, 6.8 centimetres. That circle is the space station.
flow.kid: Draw the Earth, 6.4 centimetres from the middle. Then the station, 6.8.
flow.parent: The station's circle is only 4 millimetres outside the Earth's. It almost touches the line. Alone, the child holds the string end on the dot with a finger while the grown-up helps, or tape the string end to the dot. With 2 to 4 children: one holds the dot, one draws; swap for each circle. This is how close the space station is to the ground on a map of the real sizes.

check.q: On the map the space station's circle is almost touching the Earth's circle. What does this tell you?
options: The space station is very close to the Earth, compared to the size of the Earth
The map is drawn wrongly
The space station is on the ground
check.why: The station is 400 kilometres up and the Earth is 6,371 kilometres from its middle to its edge. 400 is small next to 6,371, so the circles are very close.

flow.do: Draw two more circles. One has a radius of 26.6 centimetres, for the GPS navigation satellites. One has a radius of 42.2 centimetres, for geostationary satellites. Write the lap times beside the circles: 90 minutes, 12 hours and 24 hours.
flow.say: Now two much bigger circles. The GPS navigation satellites go round every 12 hours. The geostationary ones go round every 24 hours. Which circle is slower to go round?
flow.kid: Draw two big circles, 26.6 and 42.2 centimetres. Write the lap times.
flow.parent: The numbers are 6,371 plus 20,200, and 6,371 plus 35,786. The bigger the circle, the longer the lap.
flow.context: In this step you add the higher orbits and their lap times.

flow.do: Lay the tape measure on the floor from the Earth's middle. Put a sticker on the floor at 3.84 metres. Walk to it. This is where the Moon would be on the map.
flow.say: The Moon is 384,000 kilometres away. On our map that is 384 centimetres. Let's walk there and see how far it is from our biggest circle.
flow.kid: Put a sticker 3.84 metres from the Earth. This is the Moon.
flow.parent: The Moon's distance is about 9 times the radius of the geostationary circle. Note that on a map this size, the gap between the Earth's line and the station's line is only about the width of a fingernail. Apollo crews crossed all those rings in about the first half-day of their trip. If your room is shorter than 4 metres, lay the tape along a corridor or into the next room.

check.q: On the map, the geostationary circle is 42.2 centimetres from the middle and the Moon is 384 centimetres. About how many times farther is the Moon?
options: About 9 times
About 2 times
About 100 times
check.why: 384 divided by 42 is about 9. The Moon is about nine times as far from the Earth as the geostationary satellites are.

activities.context: This activity draws the orbits of the space station, navigation satellites and geostationary satellites to scale, with the Moon on the floor. It shows how thin the lowest orbit is and how far the higher ones are.

activities.title: Sound Needs Something: a tin-can telephone

materials.item: 2 plastic cups or empty curd cups, with smooth edges
5 metres of thin string or fishing line
a sharp pencil or a skewer, and a folded cloth or thick cardboard to press on, for the grown-up to make the holes
two buttons or two short pieces of ice-cream stick, to stop the string slipping through

activities.safety: A grown-up makes the holes with a sharp pencil tip or a skewer, pressing the cup onto thick cardboard and pushing away from their hands. Plastic cups with sharp edges should be trimmed or taped. Never use matches as stoppers.

schedule.what: Make the phone. Try it with a tight string, a loose string and a pinched string. Work out what sound needs, and what that means for space.

activities.record: Write a table with three rows: string tight, string slack, string pinched. Write how many of the 5 numbers were heard right each time, and what you heard.

flow.do: Show your child the cups and the string. Ask for a guess. Will the whisper travel along the string? What if the string is slack? Write the guesses down.
flow.say: We will make a telephone from two cups. Will a whisper go along the string? What if the string is slack? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Two cups and a string make a phone. Will a whisper travel? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the string might carry the sound?
good: The string shakes and passes the shaking on.
The sound goes along the string.
It will not work, because there is only a string.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the tin-can telephone. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up makes a small hole in the bottom of each cup with a pin. Thread the string through each hole from the outside. Tie the end to a button inside, with a double knot, so it cannot slip out.
flow.say: Push the string through the hole from outside. Tie the end to a button inside the cup, with a double knot. Do the same on the other cup.
flow.kid: Thread the string through the hole. Tie a double knot round a button.
flow.parent: The button is only a stopper, and a short bit of ice-cream stick works too. Use thin cotton thread, kite string or fishing line, not stretchy wool or elastic. Two cups, 5 metres of string, one knot at each end.
flow.context: In this step you build the telephone.

flow.do: Whisper five different numbers each time and count how many are heard right. Stand as far apart as the string allows, about 4 metres, with the string pulled tight. One person whispers into a cup. The other holds the other cup to their ear. Then let the string go slack and try again. Then pinch the string with a finger and try again.
flow.say: Pull the string tight and whisper a number into your cup. Can your friend hear it? Now let the string go loose. Now pinch the string. What changes?
flow.kid: Whisper into the cup. Try tight, slack and pinched. What do you hear?
flow.parent: Alone, the child whispers and the grown-up listens, then swap. With 2 to 4 children: one whispers, one listens, one pinches the string, one writes the score out of 5. Typical result, not promised: tight works well, slack gets fewer right, and pinched gets almost none. Expected: it works when tight, it fades or fails when slack, and it stops or goes quiet when the string is pinched. The sound is a shaking that passes along the string. A slack string cannot pass the shaking well.

check.q: Why does the phone stop working when the string is pinched?
options: The shaking cannot pass along the string past your finger
The cups get tired
The string gets longer
check.why: Sound is a shaking. It passes from one bit of the string to the next. A pinching finger stops the shaking from going on.

flow.do: Ask for what I think, what I saw and why. Then ask about space.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you hear that shows it? And why? In space there is almost nothing between the rocket and a person. Could you hear it?
flow.kid: Say what I think, what I saw and why. Could you hear a rocket in space?
flow.parent: A good answer: sound needs something to shake, such as air, string or water. In space there is almost nothing, so sound cannot travel. Astronauts talk by radio, and radio waves are a kind of light that needs nothing to carry them.

check.q: Two astronauts float outside the space station, and one shouts. Why can the other not hear her shout directly?
options: There is almost no air to carry the sound across the gap
Their helmets are too thick
It is too dark
check.why: Sound needs something to shake, such as air. In space there is almost none between the astronauts, so the shout cannot cross the gap. They use radio inside their suits.

activities.context: In this activity you make a telephone from two cups and a string and find what sound needs to travel. It shows why space is silent and why astronauts talk by radio.

activities.title: Whispering Dishes: how a curved dish gathers waves

materials.item: 2 big, deep, smooth, round steel bowls, kadais or basins, as wide as you have (30 centimetres or more)
2 low tables, stools or stacks of books to rest the bowls on their sides
a quiet room, or a quiet corner of the house
a ticking wristwatch or a phone playing a soft steady tick or tone, for a steady quiet sound if whispers are too faint (optional)

schedule.what: Set up two bowls facing each other. Whisper into one and listen at the other. Move your ear to find the best spot, and see what that says about a radio dish.

activities.record: Draw the two bowls facing each other. Mark with a cross the spot where the whisper was loudest. Write how many of the 5 numbers were heard right at the middle, at the side and with no bowl.

flow.do: Show your child the two bowls. Ask whether a whisper from one bowl can be heard from the other, 2 metres away. Ask them to guess where the best place to listen is. Write down the guess.
flow.say: Radio telescopes use a big curved dish. We will use a bowl for sound. Can a whisper cross the room from one bowl to another? Where is the best place to put your ear? Why?
flow.kid: Two bowls face each other. Can a whisper cross the room? Why?
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Remind your child that a magnifying glass gathered light from a window into one picture.
flow.context: This is the first step of the whispering dishes. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Stand the bowls on their sides on two low tables, 2 metres apart, with their open faces towards each other. Make sure both face the other's middle. One person sits behind each bowl.
flow.say: Tilt each bowl so that its open face looks straight at the other bowl. One of you whispers a number into the middle of your bowl. The other puts an ear close to the middle of the other bowl.
flow.kid: Face the bowls at each other. Whisper into one. Listen at the other.
flow.parent: The bowls need to be smooth and deep. If you cannot hear anything, bring the bowls closer, to 1 metre, and use a soft voice rather than a whisper. Switch off fans and the TV, and try it late in the evening when the house is quiet. Kitchen bowls give a small effect, not a loud one. For a steady sound, put a ticking watch or a soft phone tone at the middle of the first bowl.
flow.context: In this step you set up the two bowls.

flow.do: Whisper a number. Your friend listens with the ear right at the middle of the bowl. Then move the ear 15 centimetres to the left or right, and whisper again. Then listen with no bowl at all, just across the room. At each place, whisper five different numbers and count how many are heard right.
flow.say: Whisper the number. Can your friend say it back? Now they move their ear off to the side. Is it still loud? Now with no bowls at all?
flow.kid: Whisper a number. Try listening in the middle, at the side, and with no bowl.
flow.parent: Expected: it is clearest with the ear at the middle of the bowl, weaker off to the side, and hardest with no bowl. The curved bowl bounces the sound so that it all arrives at one spot. Alone, the child listens and the grown-up whispers, then swap. With 2 to 4 children: one whispers, one listens, one moves the ear position, one writes the scores out of 5; swap after each place. If you hear little difference, move the bowls to 1 metre, try a larger bowl, or use the ticking watch. A small difference is still a true result, so write it down.

check.q: Why is the whisper loudest when the ear is at the middle of the bowl?
options: The curved bowl bounces the sound so it all meets at one spot
The bowl makes the sound louder by itself
The middle is closer to the speaker
check.why: A curved dish reflects the waves that fall on it and sends them to one spot, the focus. Putting an ear at the focus collects the sound from the whole dish.

flow.do: Ask for what I think, what I saw and why. Then ask about the GMRT.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you hear that shows it? And why? A radio telescope is a huge dish. What do you think it gathers, and where does the receiver go?
flow.kid: Say what I think, what I saw and why. Where does a radio dish put its receiver?
flow.parent: A good answer: the dish gathers radio waves from space and bounces them to a single spot. The receiver sits at that spot, as the ear did. A bigger dish gathers more and gives a clearer signal, which is why the GMRT near Pune has dishes 45 metres wide.

check.q: Where does a radio telescope put its receiver?
options: At the spot where the curved dish gathers the waves together
On the edge of the dish
Far away from the dish
check.why: The dish bounces the waves it collects to one spot. Putting the receiver at that spot collects the signal from the whole dish.

activities.context: In this activity two bowls face each other and carry a whisper across a room. It shows how a curved dish gathers waves to one spot, which is how a radio telescope and a satellite dish work.

activities.title: Journey Strips: how many days to the Moon, the Sun's edge and Mars?

materials.item: 4 long strips of paper, each at least 35 centimetres long, cut from newspaper or old notebooks
a ruler marked in millimetres
scissors, a pencil and tape

activities.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors if the child is younger than eight.

schedule.what: Cut one strip for each journey, using 1 millimetre for each day. Lay them side by side. Compare them and ask why the journeys took such different times.

activities.record: Stick the four strips side by side on a page. Write the name and the number of days beside each one. Write how many Apollo trips fit in the Mangalyaan trip.

flow.do: Tell your child the four journeys and their days. Apollo 11 took about 4 days to land on the Moon. Chandrayaan-3 took 40. Aditya-L1 took about 126 days to reach its place near the Sun. Mangalyaan took about 320 days to reach Mars. Ask for a guess of which is the longest.
flow.say: Here are four real journeys. A trip to the Moon in 1969, India's Moon landing, India's Sun mission, and India's Mars mission. Which was the longest, and which the shortest?
flow.kid: Four space journeys. Which was shortest? Which was longest?
flow.parent: Apollo 11 landed in July 1969. Aditya-L1 was launched in September 2023 and reached its working place near the Sun in January 2024. The numbers of days are approximate.
flow.context: In this activity you cut paper strips as long as real space journeys, one millimetre for each day.

flow.do: Cut a strip 4 millimetres long for Apollo 11. Cut one 40 millimetres long for Chandrayaan-3. Cut one 126 millimetres long for Aditya-L1. Cut one 320 millimetres long for Mangalyaan.
flow.say: One millimetre for each day. Apollo 11 is 4 millimetres. Chandrayaan-3 is 4 centimetres. Aditya-L1 is 12 centimetres and 6 millimetres. Mangalyaan is 32 centimetres.
flow.kid: Cut four strips. One millimetre for each day.
flow.parent: With 2 to 4 children, each cuts one journey strip, then lay them together; alone, cut all four. Make the cuts as exact as you can. 4 millimetres is very short, about the width of a pencil. It makes a point.
flow.context: In this step you measure and cut the four strips.

flow.do: Lay the strips side by side with their left ends together. Compare them. Then count how many 4 millimetre Apollo strips would fit along the Mangalyaan strip. Ask why Chandrayaan-3 took ten times as long as Apollo 11, though the Moon is the same distance away.
flow.say: Both flew to the same Moon. Why did one journey take 4 days and the other 40? Think about the rocket and the burns.
flow.kid: Why did the same Moon trip take 4 days and 40 days?
flow.parent: About 80 Apollo trips would fit in one Mangalyaan trip (the real trip took about 300 days). Apollo used the huge Saturn V rocket, which threw the spacecraft straight to the Moon. Chandrayaan-3 used a much smaller rocket, and used many small burns of its own engine to climb in steps. The first is fast but needs a giant rocket. The second is slow but cheaper. Mangalyaan was longer because Mars is far away and the planets had to be in the right places.

check.q: Chandrayaan-3 took 40 days to reach the Moon and Apollo 11 took about 4. What is the best reason?
options: Chandrayaan-3 used a smaller rocket and made many small engine burns
The Moon was nearer in 1969
Chandrayaan-3 flew in circles to look for water
check.why: A smaller rocket cannot throw the spacecraft all the way in one push. Many small burns raise the orbit step by step. This costs time but allows a smaller, cheaper rocket.

activities.context: This activity turns four real space journeys into paper strips, so you can see how long each took. It shows why different missions take different times.

setup.caption: 1. Cut one strip for each journey. One millimetre is one day.

setup.art: Four strips of paper laid side by side, from a tiny one to a very long one, each labelled with a mission name.
setup.caption: 2. Lay the strips side by side and compare.

projects.title: Straw Rockets: what do fins and a heavy nose do?

materials.item: 3 sheets of A4 paper
a pencil, to roll the paper around
ordinary thin drinking straws, at least 1 (a fresh or wiped straw for each child who blows)
a piece of thin card, from a cereal box, for the fins
cello tape and scissors
a small ball of modelling clay, about the size of a pea
a measuring tape and a clear space about 6 metres long

projects.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors. Never aim a straw rocket at a face, and keep away from windows and glass. Test in a cleared space, let the child blow only into the straw, and never suck in through it, because the rocket or the clay could be breathed in. Keep the clay away from children under five.

schedule.what: Roll three paper rockets. Give one no fins, one fins, and one fins with a clay nose. Launch each three times. Measure and compare.

projects.record: Draw the three rockets. Under each one, write how far it flew on each try and whether it flew nose first or tumbled.

flow.do: Show your child the paper, the straw and the clay. Say that you will make three rockets, one plain, one with fins and one with fins and a heavy nose. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: We will make three paper rockets. One has no fins. One has three fins. One has fins and a clay nose. Which will fly straightest and farthest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three rockets: plain, with fins, and with fins and a heavy nose. Which flies best? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will fly the best?
good: Fins keep it pointing the right way.
A heavy nose pulls it forward.
The plain one will go farthest because it is lightest.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write the guesses at the top of the page.
flow.context: This is the first step of the straw rockets. You guess before you build.

flow.do: Roll a sheet of paper tightly round the pencil, 12 centimetres long. Tape it along the seam. Fold the top end flat and tape it shut to make the nose. Slide the tube off the pencil. Make three the same.
flow.say: Wrap the paper tightly round the pencil. Tape it down the side. Fold one end shut and tape it. That end is the nose. The open end goes on the straw.
flow.kid: Roll paper round a pencil. Tape it. Close one end to make the nose.
flow.parent: The tube should slide easily on the straw but not be baggy. A tube 12 centimetres long, about the size of a finger, flies well. Make all three the same length and width, so the test is fair.
flow.context: In this step you build three plain paper rocket bodies.

flow.do: Cut six fins from the card, each shaped like a small triangle about 3 centimetres tall. Tape three fins to the tail of the second rocket, evenly spaced. Tape three to the third rocket. Press the clay into the nose of the third rocket.
flow.say: Tape three fins to the open end of the second rocket, spaced like the spokes of a wheel. Do the same to the third one. Then press the clay into the nose of the third.
flow.kid: Tape three fins to rockets two and three. Put clay in the nose of rocket three.
flow.parent: Put the fins at the tail, the open end, with the flat edges along the tube. The clay changes the balance, and you can see this when you balance the rocket on one finger.

check.q: Why do the three rockets have the same length and width and differ only in fins and clay?
options: So that only the fins and the nose weight change
So they look the same
So they are easier to tape
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes at a time. If the rockets differed in length too, you could not tell whether the fins or the length made the difference.

flow.do: Put the first rocket on a straw. Aim along the cleared space, away from people. Blow one short, hard puff. Measure where it lands. Do three launches for each rocket. Write down the distance and whether it flew nose first or tumbled.
flow.say: Slide the rocket onto the straw. Aim at the empty space. Take a breath and blow one sharp puff. Where did it land? Did it fly nose first, or tumble?
flow.kid: Put the rocket on the straw. Aim at an empty space. Blow sharply.
flow.parent: Keep the same breath each time: one short hard puff. Do not aim at anyone. Typical, not promised: the plain rocket may fly well or may wobble and tumble, fins tend to keep the nose pointing forward, and a clay nose may fly straighter but shorter. If all three fly alike, that is a result too. Let one child blow all nine launches, or let each child blow all three rockets and compare within that child, because breath strength differs. Others mark the landing and measure. Your own results decide. Write them down as they are.
flow.context: In this step you launch each rocket three times and measure how far and how straight it flew.

flow.do: Ask for what I think, what I saw and why. Then ask how real rockets steer.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why? Real rockets fly where there is no air, so fins cannot push on anything. How might a real rocket keep pointing the right way?
flow.kid: Say what I think, what I saw and why. How does a rocket steer without air?
flow.parent: A good answer: fins keep the tail behind the nose, because air pushes on them if the rocket starts to turn sideways. That is true in air. In space there is no air, so real rockets steer by tilting their engines, or by firing small thrusters. Rockets such as India's PSLV steer partly by tilting their engine nozzles, a method called thrust vectoring.

check.q: Why can fins steer a paper rocket in a room but not a rocket in space?
options: Fins work by pushing on air, and space has almost none
Fins are too heavy in space
Fins melt in space
check.why: Fins push on the air as the rocket moves through it, and keep the tail behind. In space there is no air to push on, so rockets steer by tilting their engines or firing small thrusters.

projects.context: In this project you make three paper rockets and launch them with a straw to find what fins and a heavy nose do. It shows how a rocket stays pointed the right way in air, and why space rockets steer another way.

challenges.title: Soft Landing: land five coins from one metre without a bounce
challenges.problem: Build a lander out of home things. A stack of five coins must ride inside it. A grown-up drops the lander from one metre. The coins must stay in a tidy stack inside, and the lander must stay the right way up.
constraints: Use only paper, cups, straws, rubber bands, cotton wool or tissue, string and tape.
The lander must be no taller than 20 centimetres.
A grown-up drops it from one metre, with no throw and no push.
The five coins ride in a stack inside the lander (a paper sleeve or tube to hold them is allowed), and are still in a stack after the landing.
materials: paper cups and a paper plate
cotton wool, tissue paper or old newspaper
a plastic bag, for a parachute
general: Cushion the coins inside the lander with crumpled paper or cotton wool, so that they stop slowly.
Make legs from straws that bend and crush, so that they soak up the landing.
A parachute from a plastic bag slows the fall.
creative: Make the lander land on a ring of paper cups, like air bags.
Hang the coin box inside by rubber bands, so it floats like a seat in a car.
Combine a small parachute with crushable legs.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your lander. Build it and drop it from one metre. Change one thing, such as the legs or the cushion, and drop it again. Drop each design three times and count how many drops kept the coins in a stack. Which design did best? Why do you think it worked?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about landing gently. You build a lander that stops slowly, as India's Vikram did on the Moon.

setup.art: A child sketching two lander designs on paper: one with straw legs and one with a parachute.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch some ideas on paper.

setup.art: A lander made of a paper cup with straw legs, cotton wool inside and a stack of five coins.
setup.caption: 2. Build the lander and load the coins.

setup.art: A grown-up holding the lander at one metre against a metre ruler, ready to let go.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up lets it go from one metre.

flow.do: Read the problem and the rules together. Ask your child to sketch two or three different lander designs. Ask which part of their lander takes the first hit.
flow.say: Your lander must keep five coins safe from a one metre drop. How could you make it stop slowly instead of suddenly? Draw some ideas first.
flow.kid: Keep five coins safe from a drop. Draw some ideas first.

ask.q: What would make a lander stop more gently?
good: Soft stuff to squash.
Legs that bend.
A parachute to slow it down.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Soft Landing challenge. You plan.

flow.do: Build the first design. Put the five coins inside. A grown-up drops it from one metre onto the floor. Write down what happened to the coins and to the lander.
flow.say: Build your first lander. Load the coins. Now the drop. Did the coins stay in a stack? Did the lander stay the right way up?
flow.kid: Build your lander. Drop it from one metre. What happened to the coins?
flow.parent: Drop onto a hard floor from exactly one metre, and hold the lander level. Use the same kind of coin every time (Rs 1 or Rs 2). With 2 to 4 children, each builds their own lander and the grown-up drops all of them from the same height; then compare successes out of 3. Alone, build two designs and compare. The first number is the one to beat. Do not worry if the first one fails. Engineers learn most from a lander that fails.
flow.context: In this step you build your first design and test it.

flow.do: Change one thing about the design. Drop it again. Compare with the first drop. Do this once or twice more.
flow.say: What went wrong the first time? Change one thing only. Now drop it again. Is it better?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Drop it again. Is it better?
flow.parent: Changing only one thing at a time tells you which change helped. Look at the legs, the cushion and the parachute one by one.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative ideas, and compare them with your own. Talk about why they work.
flow.say: Here are some ideas that engineers use. Which one would you add to your lander?
flow.kid: Which idea would you add? Why?

check.q: Why does a crushable leg or a soft cushion help a lander survive a drop?
options: It makes the lander stop over a longer time, so the push on it is smaller
It makes the lander heavier
It makes the lander fall slower in the air
check.why: To stop a falling thing, the ground must take away its speed. Soft or crushable parts spread that stopping over a longer time, so the force is smaller and nothing breaks.

challenges.safety: A grown-up does the dropping and helps with the scissors. Clear the floor of people and of glass before each drop. Keep coins and plastic bags away from children under five.

challenges.title: Where Would You Build a Telescope? Pick the best place in India
challenges.problem: India wants to build a new telescope. You are the planning team. Choose one of five places, and say why it is the best for a telescope that studies faint stars in visible light and infrared.
constraints: Choose one of the five places: Hanle in Ladakh, Devasthal near Nainital, Gurushikhar on Mount Abu, Kavalur in Tamil Nadu, or a rooftop in a big city by the sea.
Use the table of things a telescope needs: clear nights, dry air, dark sky, high up, and easy to reach.
Say what you would give up in order to get what you want most.
materials: a sheet of paper and a pencil
the table of five places, drawn by your family
general: Score each place from 0 to 3 on each need. Add the scores. The highest wins.
High places have less air above them to blur the light and to hold water vapour, which blocks infrared.
A very remote place is hard to reach and costly to supply.
creative: Split the job: one telescope on a high remote mountain for the hardest work, and a smaller one near a city, for teaching.
Choose a place that has one great strength, such as extreme height, and plan for the weakness, such as hard access.
Think about a radio telescope instead, which does not care about clouds or daylight.
challenges.your_turn: Make your table of scores. Choose your site. Write three sentences to the government explaining why. Then name the one thing you would have to give up.
challenges.context: This is a planning challenge. You choose where to put a telescope, as astronomers in India have had to decide.

setup.art: A table with five rows for five places and five columns for the needs, with a child filling in scores.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the table. Score each place from 0 to 3.

setup.art: A map of India with five marked places and a star on the winner.
setup.caption: 2. Add up the scores. Mark your chosen place on the map.

flow.do: Read the problem and the five places together. Read out what is known about each. Hanle is very high, dry, cold and dark but very remote, at about 4,500 metres. Devasthal is at about 2,500 metres. Gurushikhar is at about 1,700 metres. Kavalur is at about 700 metres. A coastal city rooftop is at sea level, humid and bright.
flow.say: Five places, one telescope. Hanle is very high and dry but far away. A city rooftop is easy to reach but bright and humid. What does a telescope need most?
flow.kid: Five places. Which would be best for a telescope? Why?
flow.parent: The heights are approximate. Real telescopes stand at Hanle, Devasthal, Mount Abu and Kavalur. Each was chosen for its strengths.
flow.context: This is the first step of the telescope site challenge. You learn what is known about each place.

flow.do: Draw the table with five rows and five columns. Score each place from 0 to 3 on each need. Add up the scores and find the winner.
flow.say: Give each place a score from 0 to 3 for each need. A high score is good. Add them up. Which place wins?
flow.kid: Give each place a score. Add them up.
flow.parent: With 2 to 4 children, each argues for a different place first, then you score together. Alone, argue both sides. There is no single right answer. Hanle usually scores highest for the sky and lowest for access. A city rooftop scores highest for access and lowest for the sky. Let your child argue for the scores. They should say why.

flow.do: Write three sentences to the government. Say which place you chose and why. Say what you would give up. Read the ideas and see if one changes your mind.
flow.say: Which place did you choose? What is the one thing you gave up? Would any idea change your mind?
flow.kid: Which place did you choose? What did you give up?

check.q: Why do astronomers like to build optical and infrared telescopes high on mountains?
options: There is less air above to blur the light and block infrared, and fewer clouds
The Moon looks bigger from a mountain
Mountains are warmer
check.why: A high place has less air above it, so light is blurred less. It also has less water vapour, which blocks infrared, and often fewer clouds. The extra height does not bring you meaningfully closer to the stars.

items.p: Why does the space station not fall down to the ground?
opts: It is so high that there is no gravity
It moves sideways so fast that it keeps missing the ground as it falls
items.why: Gravity is still pulling the station, with about nine tenths of its pull on the ground. The station falls all the time, but its sideways speed of about 8 kilometres a second carries it past the curve of the Earth. Picking 'no gravity' is a very common mix-up.

items.p: Two marbles roll off the same table. One leaves slowly and one leaves fast. Say where each lands, and which one is in the air longer.
items.a: The fast marble lands farther from the table. Both marbles are in the air for about the same time, because both fall the same height with the same pull. The fast one just moves farther sideways in that time.
items.why: A strong answer says the landing places differ but the times are about the same, and gives the reason: the fall depends on height and gravity, not on sideways speed.

items.p: A satellite is always ____ towards the Earth, but its sideways speed makes it miss the ground.
items.why: An orbit is a fall that keeps missing. The satellite falls all the time, and the Earth's curve drops away below it.

items.p: To reach orbit, a rocket only has to climb high enough.
items.why: False. A rocket that stopped at 400 kilometres up would fall straight back down. Staying up needs a sideways speed of about 8 kilometres a second, and that takes most of the rocket's effort.

items.p: About how fast must a satellite near the Earth move sideways to stay in orbit?
items.why: At about 8 kilometres a second, which is about 28,000 kilometres an hour, the ground curves away as fast as the satellite falls. It is about 170 times faster than a very fast train.

items.p: Match each thing in orbit to the time that one lap takes.
pairs: A navigation satellite such as GPS
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: The higher the orbit, the longer the lap. At 36,000 kilometres a lap takes exactly one day.

items.p: In the balloon rocket test, the rocket with 20 paper clips flew a shorter distance than the one with none. Explain why.
items.a: The balloon gave the same push each time. A heavier rocket gets less speed from the same push, so it stops sooner and goes a shorter distance.
items.why: A strong answer says the push stayed the same and the weight changed, and that more weight means less speed from the same push.

items.p: Put these steps of a journey to the Moon in order, from first to last.
items: The spacecraft is caught by the Moon's gravity
Small engine burns stretch the orbit round the Earth
a: Small engine burns stretch the orbit round the Earth
The spacecraft is caught by the Moon's gravity
items.why: The rocket gets the spacecraft into orbit round the Earth. Burns then raise the orbit until the spacecraft can leave. The Moon catches it, and only then can the lander go down.

items.p: A big rocket weighs 100 tonnes at lift-off. About how much of that is propellant?
items.why: To reach 8 kilometres a second with gas that leaves at 3 to 4, a rocket must throw away most of its weight. Around nine tenths of a big rocket at lift-off is fuel and oxygen.

items.p: Sort these telescopes. Can each one work well from the ground, or must it go above the air?
items: a telescope for visible light on a high, dry mountain
items.a: see items
items.why: Radio waves and visible light pass through the air. The air blocks X-rays and most ultraviolet light, so telescopes for those must go into space.

items.p: Radio waves can pass through clouds, so a radio telescope can work on a cloudy day.
items.why: True. Radio waves go through clouds and air easily. Radio telescopes work day and night, whatever the weather.

items.p: Draw Newton's cannon on a high mountain. Show three paths of the cannonball: one that lands near, one that lands far, and one that goes right round the Earth.
items.a: A mountain on a round Earth, with a short curved path, a longer curved path, and a path that circles the whole Earth.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the faster shots land farther, and that the fastest one curves round with the Earth below it and never lands.
items.art: A blank circle for the Earth with a mountain drawn at the top.

items.p: Through your two-lens telescope, a faraway wall looked upside down. What is the reason?
opts: Simple lenses of this kind turn the picture upside down
The wall was really upside down
items.why: A simple telescope with two lenses makes an upside-down picture. This does not matter in the sky, where there is no right way up. Some telescopes add a mirror or lens to turn it round.

items.p: A light-year is a measure of ____, not of time.
items.why: A light-year is the distance that light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres.

items.p: Astronauts on the space station exercise about two hours every day. Explain why.
items.a: In orbit there is no weight to carry, so bones and muscles get weaker, because they do not have to work. Exercise gives them something to push against, which slows the loss.
items.why: A strong answer says that weightlessness removes the load on the body and exercise puts a load back.

items.p: Label the picture of a space telescope: mirror, sunshield, solar panel, antenna.
items.a: The big mirror is at the front. The sunshield is below it. The solar panel is on one side. The antenna that talks to Earth sticks out at the back.
items.why: A strong labeller puts the mirror at the front where the light enters and the sunshield between the mirror and the Sun.
items.art: A drawing of a space telescope with a big round mirror and four blank label lines.

items.p: Sound can travel through empty space.
items.why: False. Sound is a shaking that passes through air, string or water. Space has almost nothing to shake, so astronauts talk by radio.

items.p: What is space debris?
opts: Dust that comes from the Sun
Broken satellites, empty rocket stages and tiny bits that still orbit the Earth
items.why: Space debris is the junk that people have left in orbit. Even a speck moving at orbital speed can damage a satellite.

items.p: More and more satellites are launched each year, and old ones become junk. A town meeting is discussing what to do.

views.says: Every new satellite should be built to drop out of orbit when it dies, and the law should make companies do it.

views.who: Farah, who runs a small satellite company
views.says: Strict rules make launches too costly. Small companies and small countries would lose their chance to use space.
Space belongs to everyone. All countries should share the cost of tracking and cleaning up the junk.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing that someone else has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses a fact, such as: junk moves at 8 kilometres a second, so even tiny pieces cause damage, or old satellites at 36,000 kilometres stay for ages. It then admits a fair point from another side, such as the cost to small companies.
items.why: This is a real argument. Safety and shared use are set against cost and fairness, and no one answer settles it.

items.p: Satellite A orbits 500 kilometres above the Earth. Satellite B orbits 1,500 kilometres above it. Which one takes longer for one lap?
items.why: Higher satellites move slower and have a longer way round. So B takes longer for a lap.

items.p: A ship sails away from the shore, and its hull disappears before its sail. How does this show that the sea curves?
items.a: If the sea were flat, the whole ship would shrink to a dot together. Because the sea curves, the bottom is hidden behind the bulge first, and the high sail is seen last.
items.why: A strong answer says that a curve hides the low parts first, which a flat sea would not do. This is why the ground drops away below a fast-moving satellite.

items.p: At the height of the space station, there is almost no gravity.
items.why: False. At 400 kilometres up, gravity is still about nine tenths of its strength on the ground. Astronauts float because they and the station fall together.

items.p: A satellite that takes exactly one day to go round stays above the same spot. It is in a ____ orbit.
items.why: Geostationary means 'standing still over the ground'. It is about 36,000 kilometres up, above the equator.

items.p: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach the Earth. What is true when you look at the Sun?
opts: You see the Sun as it was about 8 minutes ago
You see the Sun as it is now
You see the Sun as it will be in 8 minutes
items.why: Light takes time to travel. The light that reaches your eye left the Sun about 8 minutes and 20 seconds ago.

items.p: Your front lens makes the picture brighter when it is wider, and your telescope magnifies more when the front lens has a longer focal length. Explain each in one sentence.
items.a: A wider front lens catches more light, so the picture is brighter. A front lens with a longer focal length makes a bigger picture for the eyepiece to magnify, so the telescope magnifies more.
items.why: A strong answer keeps the two jobs apart: width is about light and detail, focal length is about how big the picture is.

items.p: Put these in order of how long their light takes to reach us, shortest first.
items.why: Light from the Moon takes about 1.3 seconds, from the Sun about 8 minutes, and a signal from Voyager 1 takes close to a day.

items.p: Draw a satellite going round the Earth. Draw an arrow for the way it is moving and an arrow for the pull of gravity.
items.a: A circle for the Earth and a satellite on the circle's edge. One arrow along the path, sideways. One arrow pointing from the satellite towards the middle of the Earth.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the two arrows at right angles. Gravity pulls it towards the Earth and its speed carries it sideways, so the path curves round.
items.art: A blank circle for the Earth and a dotted ring around it.

items.p: The space station moves at about 7.7 kilometres a second. Is each of these faster or slower than the station?
items: a speck of junk 300 kilometres up
items.a: see items
items.why: Lower orbits are faster and higher orbits are slower. Anything lower than the station must move faster than it to stay up.

items.p: Rockets from Sriharikota usually launch towards the east. What is the reason?
opts: The Earth spins towards the east, so the rocket starts with some of that speed for free
The Moon is in the east
The wind always blows from the east
items.why: The Earth's surface moves eastwards. A rocket launched east gets a speed boost from the spin, which saves fuel.

items.p: Fins steer a paper rocket across a room, but they cannot steer a rocket in space. Explain why.
items.a: Fins work by pushing on the air that flows past them. If the rocket turns sideways, the air pushes the tail back behind the nose. In space there is almost no air, so fins have nothing to push on. Real rockets steer by tilting their engines or firing small thrusters.
items.why: A strong answer says that fins need air to push on, and names another way to steer.

items.p: A telescope on Earth can show the flag left on the Moon if the telescope is big enough.
items.why: False. The flag is too small to show up from 384,000 kilometres away, even in the biggest telescopes. Spacecraft circling the Moon close to the surface have photographed the landing sites.

items.p: Two stars look like one star in a small telescope but like two in a big one. What has the big telescope given?
items.why: A wider opening gives finer detail, which scientists call resolution. It also collects more light.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: The useful thing a rocket carries
The fuel and oxygen a rocket burns
A section of a rocket that drops when it is empty
The push that comes from the engine
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These four words describe how a rocket is built and how it moves.

items.p: Pick one danger that space brings for the body, and say how astronauts protect themselves from it.
items.a: Weightlessness weakens bones and muscles, and astronauts exercise two hours a day against it. Radiation can harm the body, and the Earth's magnetic field and the station's walls turn away much of it. Junk can damage the station, so it is tracked, and the station moves if a piece comes near.
items.why: A strong answer names one danger, explains what it does, and gives a way of protecting against it.

items.p: Apollo 11 took about 4 days to reach the Moon. Chandrayaan-3 took 40 days. How many times longer did Chandrayaan-3 take?
items.why: 40 divided by 4 is 10. Chandrayaan-3 used a smaller rocket and many small engine burns, which took ten times as long.

items.p: Label the picture of a two-lens telescope: front lens, eyepiece, faraway object, gap between the lenses.
items.a: The faraway object is on the left. The front lens is next to it, and the eyepiece is at the eye end. The gap is the space between the two lenses.
items.why: A strong labeller puts the big, weak lens at the front and the small, strong lens at the eye.
items.art: A drawing of a stick with two lenses on it, a faraway tree, an eye, and four blank label lines.

items.p: The 30 dishes of the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope work together like one huge ____.
items.why: Dishes spread over about 25 kilometres act together like one telescope that large.

items.p: A friend says that astronauts float because there is no gravity on the space station. What would you say to her, and what evidence would you give?
items.a: Gravity at the station's height is still about nine tenths of what it is on the ground. The station would fall straight back if it stopped moving sideways. The astronauts float because they and the station fall together round the Earth, so the floor does not push on them. The marble test shows the same kind of falling with sideways speed.
items.why: A strong answer gives the number, says what really happens, and uses the idea of falling together.

items.p: A satellite close to the ground moves sideways at only 4 kilometres a second, half the speed needed. What happens?
opts: It falls to the ground, because the ground curves away too slowly
It goes into a higher orbit
It floats at the same height for ever
items.why: At half the orbital speed, the satellite falls faster than the ground curves away, so it hits the ground. It would need about 8 kilometres a second to keep missing.

items.p: A company wants to dig up ice on the Moon and sell the water to space travellers. A meeting is discussing who may own what is dug up.

views.who: Kavitha, an engineer in a mining company
views.says: Whoever pays for the mission and does the digging should own what they dig, or no company will go.
The Outer Space Treaty says no country can claim the Moon. We need new agreements before the first mine, not after.
The Moon belongs to everyone. Its water should be shared, like the oceans, and not sold to the highest bidder.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then say one thing that someone else has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason, such as the cost of missions or the Moon as a shared place. It then agrees with a fair point from another side, such as the need for a new treaty.
items.why: This is a real, unsettled argument about law, fairness and cost.

items.p: A rocket body and its payload weigh 10 tonnes together, and the rocket weighed 100 tonnes at lift-off. What fraction of the lift-off weight was propellant?
items.why: 100 take away 10 leaves 90 tonnes of propellant. 90 out of 100 is nine tenths.

items.p: In the balloon test, 20 clips cut the flight by more than half. Use this to explain why the satellite on top of a rocket is only a few percent of its weight.
items.a: Every extra bit of weight needs extra push to move, and the push comes from fuel that also has weight and also has to be lifted. So adding payload needs more fuel, which needs even more fuel to lift it. The result is that the rocket is mostly fuel, and the payload is only a small part.
items.why: A strong answer connects the weight of the payload to the extra fuel needed, and the fuel that lifts that fuel.

items.p: A geostationary satellite has to be above the equator.
items.why: True. Only a circle above the equator can match the Earth's spin and stay over one spot. A circle tilted from the equator would swing north and south of it.

items.p: Voyager 1 moves about 17,000 times slower than light. The nearest star is about 4 light-years away. About how long would Voyager 1 take to reach it?
items.why: Light takes 4 years. Voyager is about 17,000 times slower. 4 times 17,000 is 68,000, so about 70,000 years.

items.p: Put these in order of their distance from the centre of the Earth, nearest first.
items.why: The surface is about 6,400 kilometres from the centre. The station is about 400 kilometres above that. Geostationary satellites are 36,000 kilometres above, and the Moon is about 384,000 kilometres away.

items.p: Why does a very dry mountain like Hanle make a good place for an infrared telescope?
items.a: Water vapour in the air blocks and glows in infrared light. A high, dry place has very little water vapour above it, so more infrared light reaches the telescope. It is also cold and has clear nights.
items.why: A strong answer links dryness to the blocking of infrared by water vapour.

items.p: Draw a radio dish with some waves coming in from space. Show where the waves go after they hit the dish, and where the receiver sits.
items.a: A curved dish facing upwards with parallel lines coming in, bending to meet at one point above the dish. The receiver is drawn at that point.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the dish bouncing all the waves to a single spot, with the receiver exactly there.
items.art: A curved dish drawn on a blank page with a stand and space above it.

items.p: Is each of these effects on an astronaut mostly caused by weightlessness or by radiation?
items: a higher chance of cancer later in life
items.a: see items
items.why: Without weight to carry, bones weaken and body fluids shift upwards. Radiation damages the cells in living bodies and the parts of electronics.

items.p: Light from a faraway galaxy took ten billion years to reach us. What do we see when we look at it?
opts: The galaxy as it was ten billion years ago
The galaxy as it is today
The galaxy as it will be in ten billion years
items.why: The light carries news from the time it left. Looking far away is looking back in time.

items.p: Isaac Newton asked whether the pull that drops an apple also reaches the Moon. How could he check this idea with numbers?
items.a: The Moon is about 60 times farther from the Earth's centre than an apple. Gravity should be 60 times 60 weaker there. He worked out how far the Moon should fall each second under that weaker pull, and checked that this matched the way the Moon's path curves as it moves sideways.
items.why: A strong answer says that the pull gets weaker with distance, and that the number was tested against the Moon's real path.

items.p: To stay above one spot on the equator all day, a satellite must take ____ hours to go round once.
items.why: The Earth turns once in 24 hours. A satellite that takes the same time to go round keeps up with the spinning ground.

items.p: A satellite 400 kilometres up is left alone with its engine off. Why does it slowly sink back over the years?
opts: A trace of air at that height slows it down a little all the time
items.why: There is still a very thin trace of air at 400 kilometres. It slows the satellite a little. A slower satellite is lower, and it spirals down until it burns up in the thicker air.

items.p: A telescope mirror twice as wide as another one gathers about four times as much light.
items.why: True. The light-gathering area depends on the width times itself. Twice as wide means two times two, which is four times the area.

quiz.p: Gul throws a ball sideways from the top of a cliff, and it curves down to the ground. What would she have to change for it to go all the way round the Earth?
opts: Throw it much, much faster, at about 8 kilometres a second
quiz.why: A faster throw lands farther away. At about 8 kilometres a second, the ground curves away as fast as the ball falls, so it misses the ground for ever. Height and weight are not what decides it.

quiz.p: A rocket climbs to the height of the space station. What takes most of its effort?
quiz.why: Rising 400 kilometres needs only about a third of the speed that staying there needs. Most of the effort goes into the sideways speed of about 8 kilometres a second.

quiz.p: A balloon rocket on a string flies a short way when it has paper clips taped to it. What would make it fly farther?
opts: Taking some of the clips off
quiz.why: A lighter rocket gets more speed from the same push. In the test, every extra clip shortened the flight.

quiz.p: Why is most of a big rocket's weight at lift-off made up of propellant?
opts: It must throw away a lot of gas to reach a speed greater than the gas speed, and it must lift its own fuel
Propellant is lighter than the rocket body
Rockets are built to look big
quiz.why: The gas leaves at 3 to 4 kilometres a second but the rocket needs about 9. So it must throw away most of its weight. The fuel also has to be lifted, which takes more fuel.

quiz.p: At about what height does a satellite go round the Earth in exactly one day, so that it stays above one spot?
quiz.why: At about 36,000 kilometres, a lap takes 24 hours, the same as the Earth's turn. At 400 kilometres a lap takes 90 minutes. At 384,000 kilometres, where the Moon is, a lap takes about 27 days.

quiz.p: A satellite moves from a lower orbit to a higher one. What happens to its speed and to the time of its lap?
opts: It moves slower, and a lap takes longer
It moves faster, and a lap takes longer
It moves faster, and a lap takes less time
quiz.why: Higher orbits are slower because the Earth's pull is weaker there. The satellite also has a longer way round, so a lap takes longer.

quiz.p: Two stars very close together look like one star in a small telescope. A wider telescope shows them as two. What has the wider telescope given?
quiz.why: A wider opening shows finer detail, which is called resolution. It also collects more light.

quiz.p: Why can a radio telescope work in the daytime and on cloudy days?
opts: Radio waves pass through clouds and do not need a dark sky
quiz.why: Radio waves go through air and clouds, and the Sun's brightness does not get in the way of radio dishes. They work day and night.

quiz.p: An astronaut spends six months in orbit and does no exercise. What is likely to happen to her?
opts: Her bones and muscles get weaker
Nothing, because she does not need to carry any weight
quiz.why: On Earth, bones and muscles work against gravity all day. Without that load they lose strength. This is why astronauts exercise for about two hours a day.

quiz.p: Why can a tiny fleck of paint in orbit damage a satellite?
opts: It moves at about 8 kilometres a second, so it carries a lot of energy
quiz.why: Energy rises quickly with speed. A fleck at orbital speed carries more energy than a bullet.

quiz.p: Chandrayaan-3 took 40 days to reach the Moon. What was it doing for most of that time?
opts: Firing its engine to raise its orbit round the Earth, and later to lower its orbit round the Moon
Waiting for the Moon to come near
Looking for a place to land
quiz.why: A smaller rocket cannot throw the spacecraft all the way to the Moon in one push. The spacecraft's own engine fired many times, raising its orbit step by step, and later lowering it.

quiz.p: In September 2019 the lander of Chandrayaan-2 lost contact just before touching down. What did ISRO do next?
opts: Studied what went wrong, changed the lander and its landing plan, and landed in 2023
Stopped trying to land on the Moon
Waited for another country to do it
quiz.why: ISRO learned from the failure and built Chandrayaan-3. India landed near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023.

videos.title: How the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope works
videos.why: To see the dishes of the GMRT near Pune and how many dishes act as one telescope.

videos.check: Not yet found. Look for ISRO's own mission animation, watch it, and check the dates against this unit before adding it.

applications: Geostationary satellites carry TV, phone and weather signals, and a dish on a roof stays pointed at one spot in the sky.
India's NavIC navigation satellites help ships, trains and phones find their position.
Weather satellites track cyclones in the Bay of Bengal, so coastal families can be warned in time.
Distress alert boxes on fishing boats send a position through a satellite when an engine fails far from the shore.
Satellite pictures help farmers and officials watch crops, floods, forests and water in lakes and reservoirs.
Big telescopes on mountains and in space, and radio dishes, help scientists learn how stars and galaxies are born.
Space debris tracking lets satellites and the space station move away from junk before a collision.
Exercise machines and bone studies made for astronauts help doctors understand weak bones in older people.
Water recycling systems made for space stations are used to clean drinking water in places far from pipes.
Engineers who design a soft landing for a lander use the same ideas as people who design helmets and cycle seats.

open_questions.q: How can people stay healthy on a trip to Mars and back?
open_questions.why_open: The trip takes many months each way. Nobody yet knows how to protect bones, muscles, eyes and the body from radiation for that long.

open_questions.q: Could a telescope find signs of life on a planet around another star?
open_questions.why_open: Telescopes such as the James Webb can study the air of some faraway planets. So far, nobody has found clear signs of life.

open_questions.q: What is the best way to clean up space junk?
open_questions.why_open: Ideas include nets, harpoons and lasers, but none has yet cleaned up much junk. It is hard to catch something moving at 8 kilometres a second.

open_questions.q: Can people ever travel to another star?
open_questions.why_open: The nearest star is over 4 light-years away. Ideas such as light sails have been imagined, but nobody has built one that could carry anything to another star.

open_questions.q: Who may own what is dug up on the Moon or on asteroids?
open_questions.why_open: The 1967 treaty says that no country can own the Moon, but it does not clearly say who may own what is dug up. Countries disagree.

open_questions.q: What is the cheapest safe way to put things into orbit?
open_questions.why_open: Reusable rockets and new engines are being tried. Nobody knows how cheap and safe launching can become.

open_questions.q: How much water is there on the Moon, and could people really use it?
open_questions.why_open: We know there is ice in dark polar craters, but not how much or how easily it can be dug out.

jokes.a: Thanks, I needed to lose some weight.

jokes.j: Why do satellites never get tired of falling?
jokes.a: Because they never hit the ground.

jokes.j: What do you call a lazy astronaut?
jokes.a: A space cadet who is just floating along.

jokes.j: Why did the telescope win the school prize?
jokes.a: It always saw the big picture.

jokes.j: How does the Moon cut its hair?
What do you get if you cross a rocket with a dosa?
Why was the radio dish such a good listener?
Why did the balloon rocket refuse to carry more clips?
jokes.a: It said, don't weigh me down.

jokes.j: Why did the astronaut become a baker?
jokes.a: She wanted a job with a lot of space.

maths.problem: On your orbit map, 1 centimetre stands for 1,000 kilometres. The geostationary circle is 42.2 centimetres from the middle, and the Earth's edge is 6.4 centimetres from the middle. How many kilometres above the ground is a geostationary satellite?
maths.explain: 42.2 take away 6.4 is 35.8 centimetres on the map. Each centimetre is 1,000 kilometres, so 35.8 centimetres is 35,800 kilometres.
maths.context: In the Orbit Map activity, you draw satellite orbits to scale on newspaper.
maths.why_maths: A scale lets you shrink huge distances to a map you can draw, and then turn a measure on the map back into a real distance.

maths.problem: A table is 80 centimetres high, and a marble takes about 0.4 seconds to fall to the floor. Marble A leaves the edge at 50 centimetres a second. Marble B leaves at 100 centimetres a second. How far from the table does each land? What does this show about doubling the speed?
maths.answer: A lands 20 centimetres away and B lands 40 centimetres away. Doubling the speed doubled the distance.
maths.explain: Distance is speed times time. 50 times 0.4 is 20. 100 times 0.4 is 40. Both marbles fall for the same 0.4 seconds, so the faster one covers twice as much ground in that time.
maths.context: In the Falling Sideways test, a marble rolls off a table and lands some distance away.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying speed by time predicts where a marble will land, and shows why the fall time is the same for every speed.

maths.problem: In a balloon rocket test, the average distances were: 0 clips, 300 centimetres. 10 clips, 190. 20 clips, 110. 30 clips, 60. By how much did the distance fall for each extra 10 clips? Was the fall the same each time?
maths.answer: It fell by 110, then 80, then 50 centimetres. The fall got smaller each time.
maths.explain: 300 take away 190 is 110. 190 take away 110 is 80. 110 take away 60 is 50. The first 10 clips cost the most distance, and later clips cost less because the rocket was already slow.
maths.context: In the Loaded Balloon Rocket test, you taped paper clips to a balloon rocket.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting neighbouring results shows whether a pattern is steady or changing, which a plain list of numbers hides.

maths.problem: The Moon is 384,000 kilometres away, and light travels 300,000 kilometres every second. About how many seconds does moonlight take to reach us?
maths.explain: 384,000 divided by 300,000 is a little more than 1. It is about 1.28, which rounds to 1.3 seconds.
maths.context: In the explanation about light travelling, you met a light-second.
maths.why_maths: Dividing a distance by a speed gives a travel time, and shows that even light takes time to cross space.

maths.problem: Chandrayaan-3 was launched on 14 July 2023 and landed on 23 August 2023. How many days was that? Aditya-L1 was launched on 2 September 2023 and reached its place near the Sun on 6 January 2024. How many days was that?
maths.explain: From 14 July to 31 July is 17 days, and then 23 more in August makes 40. For Aditya-L1: 28 days left in September, then 31 in October, 30 in November, 31 in December, and 6 in January. 28 plus 31 is 59, plus 30 is 89, plus 31 is 120, plus 6 is 126.
maths.context: In the Journey Strips activity, you cut one strip of paper for each space journey.
maths.why_maths: Counting days between dates lets you compare real journeys fairly.

maths.problem: Voyager 1 moves about 17,000 times slower than light. The nearest star is about 4 light-years away, which is how far light goes in 4 years. About how many years would Voyager 1 take to get there?
maths.explain: Light takes 4 years. A thing 17,000 times slower takes 17,000 times as long. 4 times 17,000 is 68,000 years.
maths.context: In the explanation about the speed of light, Voyager 1 was used as the farthest spacecraft.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying by how many times slower something is shows how far beyond our reach the nearest stars are.

maths.problem: The Devasthal telescope has a mirror 3.6 metres wide. A small school telescope has a mirror 1.2 metres wide. How many times wider is the big mirror? How many times more light does it gather?
maths.answer: 3 times wider, and 9 times more light.
maths.explain: 3.6 divided by 1.2 is 3. The light gathered depends on the area, and area grows with width times width. 3 times 3 is 9.
maths.context: In the telescope explanation, a wider opening gathers more light.
maths.why_maths: Seeing that area grows by width times width explains why a modest increase in size makes a very big difference to what a telescope can see.

maths.problem: A rocket weighs 200 tonnes at lift-off, and 180 tonnes of that is propellant. Its first stage weighs 130 tonnes in all and is dropped when empty. How much does the rest of the rocket weigh after the drop? What fraction of the lift-off weight is that?
maths.answer: 70 tonnes, which is a little more than one third.
maths.explain: 200 take away 130 is 70. 70 out of 200 is 7 out of 20, which is a little more than one third. The rest of the rocket is now much lighter, so each push speeds it up more.
maths.context: In the balloon rocket test, you saw that a lighter rocket goes farther, which is why rockets drop stages.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting the dropped stage and finding what fraction is left shows how much easier the rest of the rocket becomes to speed up.

maths.problem: A lap of the Earth at the station's height is about 42,000 kilometres. The station moves at 7.7 kilometres every second. About how many minutes does one lap take?
maths.explain: 42,000 divided by 7.7 is about 5,450 seconds. 5,450 divided by 60 is about 91 minutes.
maths.context: In the explanation of orbital speed, a lap of the station takes about 90 minutes.
maths.why_maths: Dividing a distance by a speed to get a time lets you check a number that you were told, and shows that it makes sense.

maths.problem: A Vande Bharat train runs at about 160 kilometres an hour. A satellite near the Earth moves at about 28,000 kilometres an hour. About how many times faster is the satellite?
maths.answer: About 175 times, or about 170 times faster.
maths.explain: 28,000 divided by 160 is 175. So the satellite is roughly 170 to 175 times as fast as the train.
maths.context: In the explanation of how fast and how long a lap, a very fast Indian train was used as a comparison.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one speed by another gives a plain 'how many times faster', which helps you picture a speed you have never felt.

maths.problem: In your telescope, the front lens has a focal length of 120 centimetres and the eyepiece has a focal length of 6 centimetres. It magnifies 20 times. You swap the eyepiece for a stronger one, to magnify 30 times with the same front lens. What focal length should the new eyepiece have?
maths.explain: Magnifying is the front focal length divided by the eyepiece focal length. 120 divided by 6 is 20. For 30 times, 120 divided by 30 is 4. A stronger eyepiece has a shorter focal length.
maths.context: In the two-lens telescope, magnifying depends on the focal lengths of the two lenses.
maths.why_maths: Working backwards from the magnifying you want to the eyepiece you need is how telescope makers choose their lenses.

how_we_found_out.story: More than 2,300 years ago, the Greek thinker Aristotle taught that the sky and the Earth follow different rules. Things on Earth fall to the ground. Things in the sky are made of a perfect stuff and move in circles by their own nature, so they never fall. For about 2,000 years most scholars agreed. Then Isaac Newton asked whether the pull that drops an apple might also reach the Moon. The Moon is about 60 times farther from the Earth's centre than an apple. So he worked out that the pull there should be 60 times 60, or 3,600 times, weaker. It would make the Moon fall only about a millimetre and a half each second. He compared this with the Moon's sideways speed, about one kilometre a second, and the numbers matched the curve of the Moon's path. He also imagined a cannon on a mountain, firing faster and faster. In 1687 he published this in his book, the Principia. The Moon was falling too. The sky followed the same rule as the apple.
how_we_found_out.who: Isaac Newton, an English scientist (1643 to 1727)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Aristotle taught that the heavens follow different rules from the Earth, so the Moon and the stars never fall. Newton showed that the Moon falls like an apple, only it moves sideways so fast that it keeps missing.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. Falling Sideways needs a table at least 70 centimetres high, a hard floor and a wet marble, and the example numbers are worked out from the ramp heights, so real numbers may be smaller because of friction. The loaded balloon rocket needs a smooth string and balloons of the same kind. If 30 paper clips stall the rocket, use fewer. The two-lens telescope needs weak reading glasses and a pocket magnifier, and takes patience, because the picture is upside down and a little blurry. The whispering dishes work best with smooth, deep bowls. Facts for a grown-up to check: the dates of the Chandrayaan-3 burns (1 and 5 August 2023), the Mangalyaan cost, the Aditya-L1 arrival date, and the numbers of tracked space junk objects.
